# 3.3 Transition elements

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Transition elements — 3.3.1

### The definition depends on electronic structure

For this syllabus, a transition element is a d-block element that forms one or more ions with an incomplete d subshell. An incomplete d subshell contains fewer than the full ten d electrons and is not empty. The position of an element in a broad rectangular block of the table is useful evidence, but the stated ion criterion must also be checked.

Copper illustrates why looking only at the neutral atom is insufficient. Its atom has [Ar]3d10 4s1, with a full 3d subshell, but Cu2+ has [Ar]3d9. It therefore meets the syllabus criterion. Zinc's common Zn2+ ion has [Ar]3d10, so it does not meet this criterion merely by sitting beside the transition series. A coloured appearance or metallic conductivity alone does not replace this electronic test.

Iron supplies familiar incomplete-d ions: Fe2+ is 3d6 and Fe3+ is 3d5 beyond the argon core. The electrons are counted after removing those needed to give the ion's charge. Do not interpret a Roman numeral in the ion name as a number of d electrons; it describes oxidation number.

This chapter also includes Namibian metal-extraction examples. Uranium belongs to the actinides and is discussed because the syllabus uses it in metallurgy. Its appearance beside copper and manganese in an extraction section does not make it a first-row d-block transition metal. Keep a classification claim distinct from the choice of an industrial example. These definitions connect Topic 1.2's electron configurations to the characteristic chemistry of transition ions.

### Configurations and electrons in boxes

Use s, p and d labels with their electron counts. Iron is [Ar]3d6 4s2. Its argon core represents 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6. To form Fe2+, remove the two 4s electrons, giving [Ar]3d6. Fe3+ has lost one further d electron, giving [Ar]3d5. Count total electrons as atomic number minus positive charge: iron's 26 becomes 24 in Fe2+ and 23 in Fe3+.

In electron-box notation, draw one box for each orbital. There are five equivalent d boxes. Fill them singly with the same spin direction before adding a second electron to a box; a pair in one orbital has opposite spins. For Fe2+, one valid 3d representation is [↑↓][↑][↑][↑][↑]. For Fe3+ it is [↑][↑][↑][↑][↑]. The position of the paired box within a set of equivalent orbitals is not itself a different configuration.

The neutral chromium and copper exceptions introduced in Topic 1.2 remain relevant: Cr is [Ar]3d5 4s1 and Cu is [Ar]3d10 4s1. Cu2+ loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron, producing [Ar]3d9. Do not start from an incorrectly imposed 4s2 pattern and then carry its error into the ion.

When representing an unfamiliar ion, write the atom first, remove the required electrons in the appropriate order and verify the total. Then draw the partially filled subshell with correct box number and spin pairs. A superscript is an electron count; an ion charge is a separate label. If a question asks for both notations, a correct compact configuration alone does not supply the missing orbital-box representation.

### Characteristic chemistry without a universal shortcut

Transition elements commonly show several oxidation states, form coloured compounds and act as catalysts. Their incomplete d subshells are associated with these characteristic behaviours. Outer s and d electrons are relatively close in energy, allowing different numbers to be involved in the formal electron accounting of compounds. Iron(II) and iron(III) are familiar examples of two accessible states.

Coloured transition-ion compounds interact with visible light through their electronic structure. The observed colour depends on the ion and its chemical surroundings. A copper(II) aqueous solution and an iron(III) solution need not have the same colour, and changing the species present can change the appearance. The element name alone does not specify the exact colour of any compound containing it.

Catalytic behaviour can involve changes in oxidation state during intermediate steps or interaction with reactants at a metal surface. The catalyst provides a different pathway and is regenerated overall. A homogeneous catalytic ion and a heterogeneous metal surface can therefore both be useful, with different chemical explanations for their active sites or temporary states. Topic 2.4 supplies the lower-activation-energy interpretation.

Treat these features as characteristic tendencies. They do not imply that a sample lacking visible colour cannot contain a transition element or that an arbitrary transition compound catalyses any reaction. The definition still requires the d-electron criterion, while an application needs evidence about the actual ion or catalyst. In a supplied reaction, a change from Fe2+ to Fe3+ demonstrates variable oxidation state. It does not by itself establish regeneration, which would also need to be shown before calling that reacting iron species a catalyst.

### Contrasting with calcium

Calcium is a useful typical s-block comparison. Transition metals such as iron and copper generally have greater densities and higher melting points than calcium. Density means mass per unit volume, so a density comparison describes how much mass occupies the same volume. A melting-point comparison describes the energy-related change needed to disrupt the solid structure sufficiently to become liquid.

Both calcium and these transition metals have metallic bonding and can conduct electricity. Their similarity in bonding type does not make their bond strengths, packing or densities identical. Transition-metal structures involve d as well as s electrons in metallic behaviour, and the combination of electronic structure, atom size and solid arrangement contributes to their characteristic cohesion. A high melting point should be linked to strong metallic bonding rather than to the idea that covalent molecules are being separated.

The word “typical” prevents an overextended rule. The wider d-block region includes metals with unusual melting points, and individual comparisons should use the supplied data. Do not infer that being farther right automatically gives a steadily increasing density or melting point through the entire series. An irregular numerical pattern can coexist with a useful broad contrast against calcium.

For original measurement arithmetic, a metal sample of mass 15.8 g and volume 2.00 cm³ has density 7.90 g cm⁻³. Compared with a supplied calcium density of 1.55 g cm⁻³, it is about 5.10 times as dense. That supports the qualitative density contrast but does not identify the unknown uniquely. Use an electron configuration or additional chemical evidence if identity is requested. This separates a calculated physical property from the electronic definition of a transition element.

---

## Transition elements — 3.3.2

### The Namibian examples and what an ore represents

The syllabus uses copper, manganese and uranium as Namibian examples of metal-bearing ore resources. These examples connect classroom redox, solubility and electrolysis with the processing of geological materials. They are curriculum examples, not a current list of operating mines, plant production figures or company ownership. No particular mine's present output is needed to explain their chemistry.

An ore is a naturally occurring material from which a valuable component can be extracted economically in the relevant setting. It normally includes unwanted rock and other minerals as well as the valuable metal-bearing species. The useful component may be an oxide, sulphide or another compound, rather than particles of free metal. Removing the unwanted material and recovering the desired chemical form are distinct stages.

Copper and manganese are d-block examples in this topic, whereas uranium is an actinide included for extraction chemistry. A uranium-bearing ore does not imply that its first saleable product is pure uranium metal. Concentration and chemical conversion can produce intermediate compounds for further processing. Similarly, a manganese-bearing feed may be used to make an alloy such as ferromanganese rather than pure manganese.

For a Namibian processing scenario, identify the feed, the valuable component and the requested product before selecting a method. A statement that a material contains copper does not show whether direct oxide reduction or a leaching route is suitable. Ore composition, concentration, impurities and the product specification influence the choice. Avoid inventing a named plant, a recovery percentage or a commercial claim when only a chemical outline is supplied. The following sections describe the source-backed redox principles and the particular routes required by the syllabus.

### Reduction by carbon

A metal in an oxide is already combined with oxygen and has a positive formal oxidation number. Reduction to the free metal lowers that number to zero. Carbon can remove oxygen from suitable oxides at an appropriate temperature, becoming an oxide of carbon. In electron terms the metal species gains electrons and the reducing carbon species is oxidised.

For a simple copper(II) oxide model, 2CuO(s) + C(s) → 2Cu(s) + CO2(g). Copper changes from +2 to 0 while carbon changes from 0 to +4. Under other furnace settings carbon monoxide may instead be the relevant carbon product or reducing species. For example, CuO + CO → Cu + CO2 describes carbon monoxide being oxidised as copper is reduced. State the given route rather than combining inconsistent equations.

Some oxides are too stable for a useful carbon route in the specified setting. Their metals may require electrolysis or a more reactive metal reductant. An ore may also need preliminary conversion into a suitable oxide before reduction. Sulphide roasting, for instance, can change the feed chemistry and produce sulphur dioxide; it is not the same step as reducing an oxide to metal.

Keep three purposes separate. Concentrating or preparing ore increases the useful component or changes it to a more suitable compound. Smelting can combine reduction with melting and separation of a slag. Refining then removes remaining impurities from an impure metal. A balanced reduction equation accounts for atoms and electron changes, but does not alone prove that a furnace achieves pure metal or economical recovery. Topic 2.2 supplies the electron-transfer language needed to explain why carbon is the reducing agent.

### Impure copper and ferromanganese

The required copper example starts from copper oxide, which carbon reduces to metal. Use an equation consistent with the stated carbon oxide product, such as 2CuO + C → 2Cu + CO2. The copper obtained in a practical feed can contain impurities from the ore, carbon or other processing materials. An equation showing Cu as product does not establish a purity of 100%.

Impure copper may need further refining where a high-conductivity or otherwise high-purity product is required. Electrolytic refining is one possible route, but it starts from an impure metal anode and differs from depositing metal out of a prepared leach solution. Choose the description that fits the feed actually given in the question.

The syllabus's ferromanganese example uses a mixture of iron oxide and manganese oxide reduced with carbon. The product contains both iron and manganese and is an alloy. Its purpose is not to isolate manganese as a pure element. The exact furnace equations depend on the starting oxides and the carbon oxide formed; a generic oxide label cannot supply a unique balanced equation without that information.

If iron(III) oxide and manganese(II) oxide are supplied as model feeds with CO as the carbon product, separate idealised balances are Fe2O3 + 3C → 2Fe + 3CO and MnO + C → Mn + CO. The resulting metals can enter the common alloy product, which can retain carbon and other impurities. These equations illustrate redox bookkeeping rather than a universal plant recipe. A comparison answer should name the target product, the reducing agent and the reason the first metal product may be impure. Calling ferromanganese “manganese ore” would confuse a manufactured alloy with its mineral feed.

### Leaching with sulphuric acid

Leaching uses a liquid reagent to transfer a valuable component from solid material into a solution. Sulphuric acid is the required example for suitable copper-, manganese- and uranium-bearing feeds. The resulting solution is separated from insoluble residue and prepared for later recovery. The choice of acid does not mean that each mineral dissolves equally rapidly or by the same chemical step.

Copper(II) oxide illustrates a simple acid–base route: CuO(s) + H2SO4(aq) → CuSO4(aq) + H2O(l). Copper stays in the +2 state. Leaching therefore has not produced copper metal; it has moved copper into dissolved copper-containing species. A later electron-gain step is needed to recover the free metal.

For manganese and uranium feeds, the mineral's oxidation state and structure affect what chemical treatment is needed. An acid plus any necessary redox preparation must suit the actual material. Do not infer a unique dissolution equation from an element name alone. At the syllabus's outline level, follow the metal from solid feed to dissolved species and distinguish this from the following extraction stage.

Preparing the solution includes separating residue and removing or controlling impurities that would interfere with recovery. Waste acid and dissolved metals need collection and treatment rather than uncontrolled discharge. That requirement follows from the solution's chemistry even when no named mine or legal discharge limit is supplied. Comparing leaching with carbon reduction, the former changes which phase contains the valuable species, while the latter changes a metal species to the zero-oxidation-state metal. A processing route may combine several stages, so identify each stage by its chemical function rather than calling the whole route “melting the ore”.

### Recovering metal after solution preparation

A prepared metal-bearing solution can be electrolysed to deposit a suitable metal at the cathode. For copper, Cu2+(aq) + 2e− → Cu(s). The supply delivers electrons and the copper-containing solution supplies the metal ions. Suitable electrolyte and electrode operation are necessary; the same result cannot be assumed for an arbitrary mixture of dissolved species.

Manganese recovery likewise needs a controlled process because hydrogen evolution can compete in an aqueous cell. The formal cathode accounting Mn2+ + 2e− → Mn describes the metal-forming step, but does not specify a complete operating method. This is the distinction developed in Topic 2.2 between a school selective-discharge guide and an engineered recovery process.

The uranium example uses magnesium as a chemical reducing agent after the uranium-bearing material has been separated and converted into a suitable prepared compound. It is not a direction to add magnesium to a raw acidic aqueous leach, where reaction with acid and water would compete. Magnesium loses electrons and the uranium species gains them, giving uranium metal in the specified reduction route.

For formal electron accounting with uranium(IV), U4+ + 4e− → U and 2Mg → 2Mg2+ + 4e− show a two-to-one magnesium/uranium amount relationship. Here U4+ represents uranium in the prepared reacting compound, not a claim of free bare ions in an aqueous metal-making experiment. The actual compound supplies the accompanying anions and final salt products. The syllabus requires the reduction principle and reductant, rather than plant-specific preparation details. These examples show that leaching, solution purification and final metal reduction are separate operations; producing a dissolved metal species does not by itself complete extraction of the pure metal.

### Monitor a pollutant and control its route

Metal extraction can transfer unwanted substances into gases, liquids or solid residues. Roasting a sulphide-containing feed in oxygen can release sulphur dioxide, an air pollutant. Acid leaching can leave acidic liquid containing dissolved metals. Crushing, handling and high-temperature operations can release airborne particles that contain metal-bearing material. Each pathway needs a corresponding monitoring and control approach.

For sulphur dioxide, measure the gas stream and use an appropriate capture or treatment process. Where a sulphuric-acid manufacture stage is included, it can convert a sulphur dioxide feed into a useful product; this still requires control of emissions. A particulate filter alone does not necessarily remove a dissolved or gaseous pollutant. Conversely, a gas absorber does not automatically remove solid dust throughout a site.

For leach waste, monitor acidity and metal concentrations in collected liquids, with treatment appropriate to the actual solution. Neutralisation can reduce acidity, but a neutral pH does not prove that toxic metal species are absent. Some may remain dissolved or be transferred into a solid sludge that itself needs controlled handling. Identify the pollutant before choosing a measure of successful treatment.

For metal-bearing dust, capture particles at relevant sources and limit uncontrolled transport during handling. The risk depends on composition, particle release and exposure, so do not treat a named metal as harmless merely because the ore is solid. In a supplied Namibian processing scenario, link a specific control to a named waste pathway and explain how monitoring shows whether that control works. No invented discharge threshold or legal claim is needed for the chemical reasoning. Waste control is part of evaluating the process rather than an unrelated sentence appended to the extraction equation.

### Benefits and limitations of recycling

Ore deposits are finite on human production timescales. Extraction removes material from a particular geological resource, and the remaining ore may become more difficult or costly to process as composition changes. Recycling recovers metal from used products or manufacturing scrap and can reduce the need to extract fresh ore. It does not recreate the geological deposit.

Benefits can include reduced demand for mining, lower use of some extraction stages and less associated waste. The energy saving depends on the metal and recycling route; avoid claiming the same percentage for all metals without data. A relatively clean metal scrap stream can require less chemical reduction than converting an oxide ore into metal, because much of the metal is already in a useful oxidation state.

Problems arise in collecting scattered products, separating different metals and removing contamination. An alloy cannot necessarily be melted directly into a product requiring a different composition or very high purity. Some valuable material is lost during sorting or processing, and recycling itself needs energy and waste controls. A high recovery percentage is useful evidence, but purity and the intended final product also matter.

For a decision, use a named criterion and supplied data. If a recycler collects 1.00 tonne of metal-bearing scrap and recovers 0.800 tonne of acceptable product, the mass recovery is 80.0%. The unaccepted fraction has not vanished; it may include residue, unrecovered metal or impurities that need handling. Recycling can be beneficial while still leaving a need for some fresh material. A reasoned judgement includes avoided extraction, process energy, recovery losses, collection and product quality rather than assuming that calling a route recycling automatically makes its impacts zero.

title: 3.3 Transition elements — practice tasks and worked answers

# 3.3 Transition elements — practice tasks and worked answers



## ITEM-8224-3.3-P01

7 marks · Bloom: Apply

Identify one correct option per question. [7]
1. The syllabus criterion refers to a d-block element forming an ion with: A an incomplete d subshell; B any full shell; C no electrons; D a negative nucleus.
2. Fe2+ from Fe [Ar]3d6 4s2 is: A [Ar]3d4 4s2; B [Ar]3d6; C [Ar]3d8; D [Ar]3d5.
3. Cu2+ is 3d9. This means its d subshell: A is full; B is empty; C is incomplete; D holds only two electrons.
4. Fe2+ and Fe3+ illustrate: A identical oxidation state; B isotope variation; C neutron transfer; D variable oxidation states.
5. Compared with calcium, iron typically has: A higher density and melting point; B lower density and melting point; C no electrical conductivity; D a molecular solid structure.
6. A catalyst is distinguished from a consumed reducing reagent by: A absence from all steps; B regeneration overall; C an assumed colour; D lack of interaction with reactants.
7. The 3d5 box occupancy consistent with singly filling equivalent orbitals is: A [↑↓][↑↓][↑][ ][ ]; B [↑↓][↑][↑][↑][↑]; C [↑][↑][↑][↑][↑]; D [↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑↓].



### Worked answer

Key: 1 A, 2 B, 3 C, 4 D, 5 A, 6 B, 7 C; one mark per correct option.
1. A is the ion criterion. B ignores d occupancy; C describes a fully stripped atom; D contradicts nuclear charge.
2. B removes two 4s electrons. A removes the wrong subshell first; C adds d electrons; D removes three electrons overall.
3. C is nine of a possible ten. A needs ten; B needs zero; D confuses one orbital with the subshell.
4. D concerns +2 and +3. A ignores the difference; B concerns neutrons; C describes neither ion conversion.
5. A is the typical comparison. B reverses it; C ignores metallic conduction; D assigns an inappropriate molecular structure.
6. B is the catalytic distinction. A wrongly excludes temporary participation; C is not sufficient evidence of catalysis; D removes the pathway interaction.
7. C has five parallel single occupancies. A pairs prematurely; B contains six electrons; D contains ten.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: key, correct option, distractor, error. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-3.3-P02

8 marks · Bloom: Apply

Explain the following linked electronic and extraction examples. [8]
(a) Write Fe2+ in core notation and construct its five-box 3d occupancy. [2]
(b) Explain what Fe2+/Fe3+ shows about oxidation states and why it does not alone prove catalytic action. [2]
(c) Write the cathode half-equation for copper deposition from a prepared aqueous Cu2+ leach. [2]
(d) Explain the electron-transfer roles when magnesium reduces a prepared uranium compound to metal. [2]



### Worked answer

Part (a): [Ar]3d6 [1]; five d boxes [↑↓][↑][↑][↑][↑] with correct electron count and opposite-spin pair [1].
Part (b): different iron oxidation states show variable oxidation state [1]; catalysis also requires an appropriate rate effect and regeneration, which the two labels alone do not establish [1].
Part (c): Cu2+(aq) + 2e− → Cu(s). Correct species/states [1]; electron/charge balance [1].
Part (d): magnesium loses electrons and is oxidised [1]; the uranium species gains electrons and is reduced [1]. This concerns a prepared compound, not direct magnesium addition to an arbitrary acid leach. Each bracket is a separate creditworthy point.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: part, mark, creditworthy point. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-3.3-P03

5 marks · Bloom: Apply

Calculate and interpret the properties of an original iron sample with mass 15.8 g and volume 2.00 cm³. Take calcium’s comparison density as 1.55 g cm⁻³. Iron atoms have [Ar]3d6 4s2. [5]
(a) Calculate the iron sample density and its ratio to the calcium value, to three significant figures. [2]
(b) Give the Fe2+ configuration. [1]
(c) Use its d occupancy to state why iron meets the syllabus transition-element criterion. [1]
(d) State the characteristic property shown by the existence of Fe2+ and Fe3+. [1]



### Worked answer

(a) Equation density = mass/volume; working 15.8/2.00 = 7.90 g cm⁻³ to three significant figures [1]. Ratio = 7.90/1.55 = 5.10, dimensionless to three significant figures [1]. Units are already consistent and need no conversion; this supports a higher-density comparison with calcium.
(b) [Ar]3d6 [1], after removing the two 4s electrons.
(c) It forms an ion with an incomplete d subshell [1].
(d) Variable oxidation states [1].



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: equation, working, answer, unit, significant figures. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.

# 3.4 Group 17

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Group 17 — 3.4.1

### Colours must carry a phase and solvent

At room temperature and pressure, chlorine is a pale green or yellow-green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine is a grey-black crystalline solid. Bromine above its liquid is a red-brown vapour. Iodine produces a violet vapour when warmed. A description such as “iodine is purple” is therefore incomplete unless it identifies the vapour or a suitable solution rather than the ordinary solid.

In water, chlorine is usually described as pale green and bromine as orange to brown, with intensity depending on concentration. Aqueous iodine is brown. Iodine is much more soluble in an aqueous iodide solution than in pure water, but the resulting iodine-containing solution is still brown in the usual observation. The iodide ions themselves are colourless; do not assign iodine's colour to a halide salt simply because both contain the same element.

In a suitable non-polar organic solvent, iodine gives a violet or purple solution. Bromine gives an orange/red-brown solution, while chlorine remains pale green in a sufficiently concentrated sample. State the solvent when using colour to interpret a displacement experiment. Brown aqueous iodine and purple organic iodine are not contradictory observations and do not indicate two different elemental halogens.

Colour evidence supports identification but needs context. A very dilute coloured species may appear almost colourless, and a mixture of halogens or coloured reagents can give a less straightforward appearance. Record the actual phase, solvent and observed colour before naming the product. A change of layer colour after adding an organic solvent may reflect redistribution into that solvent rather than an extra redox step. This distinction connects the physical observations here to the iodide oxidation test in Topic 2.2.

### The state trend follows phase-transition temperatures

Compare the three halogens at the same room temperature and pressure. Chlorine is above its boiling point and is a gas. Bromine lies between its melting and boiling temperatures and is a liquid. Iodine is below its melting temperature and is a solid. The trend is therefore gas to liquid to solid from chlorine to iodine under that common setting.

The increasing melting and boiling temperatures indicate that more thermal energy is needed to separate the particles sufficiently for the less condensed phase. These are molecular elements: Cl2, Br2 and I2. The change in state does not arise because iodine alone has become an ionic lattice. Nor does a halogen's increasing atom count down the table mean that its ordinary elemental molecule contains more than two atoms.

The distinction between liquid and vapour can be seen for bromine, where vapour exists above the liquid. A liquid does not need to be at its boiling point for some molecules to enter the gas phase. Similarly, iodine can sublime from solid to vapour, giving the characteristic violet appearance without requiring that a visible liquid first collects in an ordinary open demonstration.

Use a specified temperature when inferring a state. If an unfamiliar halogen is predicted to have a higher boiling point than bromine, that alone does not fix whether it is liquid or solid at room temperature: its melting point is also needed. The stated chlorine/bromine/iodine sequence uses both transitions. In a data question, locate the room temperature relative to each pair of phase-transition temperatures instead of treating the group name as a fixed state. This prepares the intermolecular explanation of volatility in the next section.

### Explaining volatility through intermolecular attractions

Volatility describes how readily a substance enters the vapour phase. At comparable temperature and pressure, chlorine is more volatile than bromine, and bromine is more volatile than iodine. The molecules become larger down this sequence and contain more electrons. Their electron clouds are more readily distorted, so temporary dipole–induced dipole attractions become stronger.

More energy is then needed to separate molecules. Boiling temperature rises, and the tendency to escape into vapour at a given temperature is reduced. Link the greater molecular electron population to stronger dispersion attractions rather than merely saying that iodine is heavier. Mass and electron count correlate in this series, but intermolecular attraction is the relevant physical mechanism.

The X–X covalent bond inside a molecule is not broken during ordinary melting or vaporisation. An iodine vapour contains I2 molecules rather than being defined as free iodine atoms. Consequently, comparing I–I and Cl–Cl bond energies does not explain their boiling-point trend. The intermolecular and intramolecular changes are different even though both involve the same element symbols.

If interpreting a mass-loss demonstration, control temperature, exposed surface, time and airflow before comparing how readily material enters vapour. Faster loss of one sample can otherwise reflect a different setup. An original numerical example in which a solid loses 0.200 g over 10.0 minutes has average mass-loss rate 0.0200 g min⁻¹, but that rate alone cannot reveal a universal boiling point. Use the state observations and molecular model together. Topic 1.3 supplies the dispersion-force explanation, and Topic 5.1 develops the measurement controls needed to compare rates.

---

## Group 17 — 3.4.2

### Halogen displacement as a redox comparison

An oxidising agent accepts electrons from another species. For a halogen X2, the reduction half-equation is X2 + 2e− → 2X−. Oxidising strength decreases from chlorine to bromine to iodine. A stronger member can oxidise the halide ions of a weaker member in the usual aqueous displacement comparison.

Thus Cl2(aq) + 2Br−(aq) → 2Cl−(aq) + Br2(aq), and chlorine similarly oxidises iodide to iodine. Bromine can oxidise iodide: Br2(aq) + 2I−(aq) → 2Br−(aq) + I2(aq). Iodine does not displace chlorine or bromine from their halide solutions under the ordinary comparison. In each successful displacement, the starting halogen is reduced to its halide and the starting halide is oxidised to elemental halogen.

Colour changes can help identify the new element, but interpret them using phase and solvent. Liberating iodine gives brown colour in the aqueous system or violet in a suitable organic layer. Bromine gives an orange/brown appearance. The original added halogen may also contribute colour, especially if present in excess, so an observation should be connected to a balanced redox change rather than judged by a remembered colour alone.

The atom-level explanation uses the group trend in attraction for an incoming electron: greater distance and shielding down the group reduce the effective attraction at the outer region. Do not confuse elemental oxidising strength with halide reducing strength. I− loses electrons more readily than Br− or Cl− in this comparison, so the halide trend is the reverse. Topic 2.2 provides the oxidation-number and agent terminology that makes the two roles unambiguous.

### Reaction with hydrogen

Hydrogen and a halogen form a hydrogen halide: H2 + X2 → 2HX. In the familiar comparisons, fluorine reacts extremely vigorously, chlorine can react explosively when triggered by light, bromine needs heating for a useful reaction, and iodine gives a reversible change at elevated temperature. The stated initiation or heating belongs with the observation; an unlit hydrogen/chlorine mixture is not equivalent to one exposed to strong light.

For chlorine, H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g). The product here is hydrogen chloride gas. Dissolving it in water gives hydrochloric acid, a different physical description. For bromine vapour, H2(g) + Br2(g) → 2HBr(g). For heated iodine, H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), with reactants and product present in the equilibrium mixture at that temperature.

The energy account involves breaking H–H and X–X bonds and forming two H–X bonds. A reaction's overall enthalpy depends on all these terms. A weak X–X bond alone does not prove that its hydrogen reaction must be the most vigorous. The activation barrier and the strength of the new hydrogen–halogen bonds also matter.

Describe the trend without promising a particular yield from reaction vigour. A fast initiated reaction and a high equilibrium conversion are different ideas. For iodine at a stated temperature, reversibility limits the final composition even though HI forms. Increasing temperature can change both rate and composition, so use any supplied enthalpy information for the latter. These distinctions connect the hydrogen reactions with the energetics, equilibrium and kinetics already taught, rather than replacing chemical explanation with a list of dramatic observations.

### Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides

Thermal stability describes resistance to decomposition on heating. For the hydrogen halides the usual order is HF, HCl, HBr, HI from most to least thermally stable. For the three heavier examples in the main comparison, HCl is more stable than HBr, which is more stable than HI. The order concerns the H–X bond in the molecule rather than attractions between different HX molecules.

The halogen atom becomes larger down the group. The bond to hydrogen is longer, and effective orbital overlap is reduced. The H–X bond is weaker and requires less energy to break. HI therefore decomposes more readily on heating than HCl in the qualitative comparison. Fluorine's small size and strong H–F bond place HF at the stable end.

Do not transfer this stability order to boiling points. Boiling separates molecules and can involve special intermolecular attractions, whereas thermal decomposition breaks chemical bonds. A compound may have a relatively high boiling point without its covalent bond being the most resistant to breaking in the group comparison. Name the process before selecting the bond-energy or intermolecular explanation.

Thermal stability also differs from aqueous acid strength. Ionisation in water depends on interactions with the solvent as well as bond breaking. A statement about HI being less thermally stable is not itself a pH calculation, and a strong acid label does not mean it has a stronger H–X covalent bond. For a question about heating, refer to bond length, overlap and dissociation energy. If decomposition is represented reversibly, the measured extent also depends on temperature and the maintained mixture, so a lower stability does not mean that all HI vanishes instantly at room temperature.

### Interpreting bond-energy evidence

Use the supplied bond energies to test the thermal-stability explanation. The NSSCAS Data Booklet gives H–Cl, H–Br and H–I dissociation values of 431, 366 and 299 kJ mol⁻¹. They fall down the group, agreeing with the order HCl > HBr > HI in resistance to thermal decomposition. The values describe energy needed for gaseous bond breaking, so retain that state and process.

For an original numerical comparison, H–Cl requires 431 − 299 = 132 kJ mol⁻¹ more energy to dissociate than H–I using those data. The difference quantifies a bond-strength comparison. It does not say HCl reacts 132 times more slowly or establish a precise decomposition temperature. Rate and composition need further information.

If asked for the energy to dissociate a specified amount, multiply the molar value by moles of bonds. Breaking 0.0100 mol of H–I bonds at 299 kJ mol⁻¹ requires 2.99 kJ. This bond-breaking quantity is positive. Forming the same bond from separated gaseous atoms would have the opposite sign for matching endpoints.

When comparing different hydrogen reactions, use the full broken-minus-formed bond-energy account rather than just this H–X list. For thermal stability the H–X strength is the key qualitative evidence. For the enthalpy of H2 + X2 forming 2HX, both reactant bonds and both product bonds contribute. This is why a table can support one conclusion directly but require additional data for another. Quote the relevant values, identify the energy basis and give a chemically bounded inference. In a proposed decomposition equation such as 2HI → H2 + I2, count two H–I bonds broken and both new product bonds formed before estimating the overall heat change. The calculation method follows Topic 2.1, while the distinction between a threshold and rate follows Topic 2.4.

---

## Group 17 — 3.4.3

### Two distinct halide comparisons

For the precipitation comparison, acidify the halide sample with dilute nitric acid and add aqueous silver nitrate. Ag+(aq) + X−(aq) → AgX(s). The chloride precipitate is white, bromide cream and iodide yellow. Follow with aqueous ammonia. In the board's qualitative-analysis notes, AgCl is soluble in dilute ammonia, AgBr is partially soluble in dilute ammonia and AgI is insoluble in dilute ammonia. AgBr dissolves more fully in concentrated ammonia. Use a fresh portion where needed to keep the ammonia strength and precipitate identity clear.

These observations concern the precipitated halide and its subsequent interaction with ammonia. They are not the colours of elemental chlorine, bromine or iodine. Nitric acid avoids adding chloride from hydrochloric acid and removes interfering carbonate in the standard test. Explain a conclusion from both precipitation and the ammonia observation, rather than colour alone.

Concentrated sulphuric acid gives a different comparison. A chloride salt can liberate HCl by an acid–base reaction, for example NaCl + H2SO4 → NaHSO4 + HCl. There is no corresponding oxidation of chloride in this school comparison. Bromide first yields HBr, which can reduce the acid: 2HBr + H2SO4 → Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O. Bromine gives orange/brown colour or fumes.

Iodide is the stronger reducing halide and forms iodine, visible as dark solid or violet vapour, while sulphur can be reduced to SO2, S or H2S. One possible balance is 8HI + H2SO4 → 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O. The different products depend on the mixture; they should not be described as a single exclusive endpoint. Distinguish acid displacement from redox by checking oxidation numbers: halide rises from −1 to 0 when its element forms, while sulphur falls from +6 in the acid. These observations are chemical evidence, not instructions to identify gases by direct smelling.

---

## Group 17 — 3.4.4

### Cold and hot alkali give different oxyanions

Disproportionation is a redox change in which the same element is oxidised and reduced. Chlorine begins at oxidation number zero in Cl2. In cold dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide it gives chloride and chlorate(I): Cl2(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Cl−(aq) + ClO−(aq) + H2O(l). Chlorine falls to −1 in chloride and rises to +1 in ClO−.

Including the spectator sodium gives Cl2 + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H2O. This is the cold dilute alkali equation; attach those qualifications to the product. The I in chlorate(I) is a Roman numeral for chlorine +1 and does not refer to the element iodine. Topic 2.2 established this naming convention.

With hot concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, the product is chlorate(V): 3Cl2 + 6OH− → 5Cl− + ClO3− + 3H2O. One chlorine atom rises from 0 to +5, losing five electrons formally; five chlorine atoms fall from 0 to −1, together gaining five. The 5:1 chloride-to-chlorate(V) amount ratio is therefore consistent with electron balance.

The equations also conserve atoms and total charge. Do not replace ClO− by ClO3− in the cold equation without changing coefficients and the reaction setting. Both oxyanions have overall charge −1, but their chlorine oxidation numbers differ. Distinguish the formal oxidation number from ion charge when explaining why the hot reaction still counts as disproportionation. A correct conclusion names both the oxidised and reduced chlorine products, rather than saying only that chlorine changes oxidation state. Heat and concentration are part of the stated comparison and must travel with the products in a stand-alone answer.

### pH changes the chlorine-containing mixture

Chlorine water contains an equilibrium mixture described by Cl2(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ H+(aq) + Cl−(aq) + HOCl(aq). HOCl is chloric(I) acid, also called hypochlorous acid. Increasing H+ concentration shifts this balance towards the left in the stated mixture; removing H+ by adding alkali favours the right-hand side. Apply the concentration change explicitly rather than merely saying that pH affects chlorine.

HOCl can transfer a proton to water. The simplified representation is HOCl(aq) ⇌ H+(aq) + ClO−(aq). At higher pH, lower H+ concentration favours ClO−; at lower pH, HOCl has a larger share of that pair. This is a qualitative speciation comparison. Chlorine remains at oxidation number +1 in both HOCl and ClO−, so that proton-transfer balance is not itself a redox change. The element’s chemical form changes without changing its formal oxidation number. No numerical weak-acid dissociation calculation is needed to follow the proton-transfer and concentration reasoning.

Combining chlorine's water reaction with hydroxide consumption gives the cold-alkali chloride/chlorate(I) balance. The hot concentrated alkali product also depends on the higher-temperature chemistry already stated; pH alone is not a reason to relabel every alkaline sample chlorate(V). Keep temperature, concentration and time context where the product distinction requires it.

Acidifying a mixture containing chloride and chlorate(I) can release chlorine: ClO− + Cl− + 2H+ → Cl2 + H2O. This explains a relevant chemical hazard of combining chlorine-containing bleach with acid. It is not necessary to invent a treatment recipe to explain the reaction. In water-treatment reasoning, identify which chlorine-containing species is present and how pH changes its relative amount, rather than assuming that the dissolved element and the oxyanion are chemically identical. Topic 2.3 provides the concentration-response logic, while Topic 2.2 supplies the oxidation-number balance.

---

## Group 17 — 3.4.5

### Why chlorine can disinfect water

Chlorine reacts with water to form chlorine-containing oxidising species, including HOCl. These can damage biological material and help inactivate microorganisms. The useful treatment role follows oxidising chemistry, rather than chlorine simply colouring the water or acting as a physical filter. A reaction that destroys a coloured organic substance can show related chemistry without being a direct measurement of water quality.

pH affects the relative amounts of HOCl and ClO−. At higher pH the ClO− fraction is larger; at lower pH HOCl forms a larger fraction of that pair. HOCl is generally the more effective disinfecting species in this comparison. The concentration balance therefore matters to the operation as well as the presence of an oxidant in principle. Temperature and the substances already present in the water can also affect the required treatment performance.

An effective water-treatment process controls addition, contact and monitoring. Some oxidant can be consumed by other reacting material, so the amount added is not identical to the amount remaining available after contact. A specified residual measurement is evidence about the treated water at that stage, not a claim that the same amount was active throughout the earlier process.

Chlorination does not itself remove every dissolved salt or solid particle. Other treatment stages can address suspended material and chemical contaminants. Explain the particular function rather than promising complete purification from a single chemical. At this syllabus level, relate chlorine-water reactions and pH to disinfection, with no invented household dose or plant-specific numerical operating limit. The same chemistry helps explain why the water-treatment question needs the identity of active species and relevant concentration information. Two waters with the same total added chlorine can differ in the oxidant remaining after other substances have reacted with it.

### Useful compounds and environmental consequences

Halogens and their compounds have several different industrial roles. Chlorine-containing oxidants are used in bleaching. Chloroethene is used to manufacture poly(chloroethene), PVC. Some halogenated hydrocarbons have been used as solvents, refrigerants or aerosol propellants because of their physical properties. These are examples of chemical uses, not a claim that all halogenated compounds are interchangeable.

A useful property can also create an environmental problem. Some chlorofluorocarbon refrigerants are sufficiently stable in the lower atmosphere to persist and reach the stratosphere. Ultraviolet radiation can release chlorine radicals, which participate in catalytic ozone destruction. The radical can be regenerated through a cycle, so one chlorine-containing species can affect more than one ozone molecule. Topic 2.4 explains regeneration; Topic 4.3 develops the relevant halogenated-carbon chemistry.

Do not infer the same environmental behaviour for every compound containing chlorine or fluorine. Stability, reactions, breakdown products and where a substance is released all matter. A proposed substitute can reduce one impact while leaving others that need evaluation. A chemical comparison should identify the particular compound and evidence, rather than treating a familiar trade category as a complete environmental assessment.

For PVC, the presence of chlorine in a manufactured polymer differs from chlorine gas used as a disinfectant. The form of an element affects its properties and exposure pathways. For solvent use, the value of dissolving suitable substances should be considered alongside persistence and waste handling where data are supplied. No current production figure or regulatory claim is required here. The syllabus asks for industrial importance and environmental significance, so state both the useful function and a chemically connected consequence.

### Bleaching and the Namibian treatment application

Chlorine-containing bleach reacts chemically with colour-causing substances. Oxidation changes their structures and can remove the visible colour. The colour loss is therefore not simply a result of adding extra water or transferring a dye to a different layer. A comparison with a dilution control can distinguish physical dilution from a reacting oxidant where the experimental evidence supports that interpretation.

Moisture matters in the ordinary chlorine-bleaching description. Chlorine reacts in water to give HOCl-containing mixtures; these species supply the oxidising action. A damp coloured material can therefore respond differently from a dry one. Do not attribute the effect to free atomic oxygen being stored inside a bottle without an appropriate chemical model. The chlorine-water equation and oxidant identity provide the more useful account.

The syllabus links this chemistry to water treatment in Namibia. The chemical role remains oxidation and disinfection in a controlled treatment process. A local setting does not change the equations or justify inventing a named plant's operating numbers. Relevant evidence includes pH, oxidant concentration, what other material consumes the oxidant and how treatment performance is monitored.

Bleaching a test material and disinfecting water are related applications but different performance tests. Removing a visible colour does not prove that a water sample satisfies every quality criterion. Conversely, a disinfecting concentration need not remove all colour from every mixture. In an explanation, name the oxidising species, the chemical change it causes and the particular result being assessed. This connects a visible classroom observation with the public-treatment application while keeping the limits of each observation clear.

# 3.4 Group 17 — practice tasks and worked answers



## ITEM-8224-3.4-P01

8 marks · Bloom: Apply

Identify one correct option per question. [8]
1. Iodine vapour is: A violet; B white; C green; D blue.
2. Bromine at room temperature and pressure is: A gas; B liquid; C giant covalent solid; D ionic solution by definition.
3. From Cl2 to I2 dispersion attractions generally: A vanish; B decrease; C increase; D become covalent bonds between all molecules.
4. The least volatile of Cl2, Br2 and I2 at comparable settings is: A Cl2; B Br2; C all equal; D I2.
5. Chlorine with aqueous bromide produces: A Br2; B I2; C chlorine ions at oxidation number +7; D no redox change.
6. Bromine with aqueous iodide produces: A Br− only with no other product; B I2 and Br−; C chlorine; D oxygen necessarily.
7. An aqueous iodine observation is usually: A violet in all solvents; B colourless because iodide is colourless; C brown; D silver-white.
8. Iodine cannot ordinarily displace bromine from bromide because: A I2 is more volatile; B Br− lacks electrons; C iodine is an ionic metal; D iodine is the weaker oxidising agent.



### Worked answer

Key: 1 A, 2 B, 3 C, 4 D, 5 A, 6 B, 7 C, 8 D. One mark per correct option.
1. A is the vapour colour. B is not iodine vapour; C suggests chlorine; D confuses an iodine/starch result.
2. B is the specified state. A ignores its phase-transition temperatures; C assigns a wrong structure; D confuses pure element and solution.
3. C follows larger polarisable electron clouds. A removes attractions; B reverses the trend; D confuses intermolecular attraction with covalent networking.
4. D has strongest dispersion attractions. A chooses the most volatile; B is intermediate; C ignores the state trend.
5. A follows oxidation of Br−. B introduces iodine absent from the system; C assigns an unrelated oxidation state; D ignores displacement redox.
6. B is the balanced redox outcome. A omits the oxidised iodine product; C introduces absent chlorine; D invents a required water-oxidation product.
7. C fits the aqueous context. A ignores solvent dependence; B confuses iodine and iodide; D is the wrong material appearance.
8. D compares oxidising strengths. A does not explain the electron-transfer direction; B is false; C misclassifies iodine.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: key, correct option, distractor, error. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-3.4-P02

8 marks · Bloom: Apply

Explain the halogen observations in these linked parts. [8]
(a) State the room-temperature state and vapour colour of iodine. [2]
(b) Explain why iodine is less volatile than chlorine, referring to intermolecular attraction. [2]
(c) Write the balanced ionic equation for chlorine displacing bromine from aqueous bromide. [2]
(d) Explain why the reverse displacement using bromine and chloride is not expected in the ordinary comparison. [2]



### Worked answer

Part (a): solid [1]; violet vapour [1].
Part (b): iodine’s larger electron cloud is more polarisable [1], giving stronger dispersion attractions and requiring more energy for molecular separation [1].
Part (c): Cl2(aq) + 2Br−(aq) → 2Cl−(aq) + Br2(aq). Correct species [1]; balance/charges [1].
Part (d): bromine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine [1], so it does not oxidise chloride to chlorine under the stated ordinary comparison [1]. Each bracket is a separate creditworthy point.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: part, mark, creditworthy point. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-3.4-P03

5 marks · Bloom: Apply

Calculate and interpret this original iodine observation. A sample loses 0.200 g as violet vapour over a stated interval; take I2 molar mass as 254 g mol⁻¹. [5]
(a) Calculate the amount of I2 entering the vapour, to three significant figures. [2]
(b) State iodine’s ordinary room-temperature state and its vapour colour. [1]
(c) State whether chlorine or iodine is more volatile under comparable settings, linking the choice to dispersion attractions. [1]
(d) State which is the stronger oxidising agent in the usual halide displacement comparison. [1]



### Worked answer

(a) Equation n = m/M; working 0.200/254 = 0.000787402 mol [1]. Answer 0.000787 mol, or 7.87 × 10⁻⁴ mol, to three significant figures [1]. Units g cancel against g mol⁻¹, so no mass conversion is needed.
(b) Iodine is a solid at room temperature and gives violet vapour [1].
(c) Chlorine is more volatile because its molecules have weaker dispersion attractions [1].
(d) Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent [1].



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: equation, working, answer, unit, significant figures. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.

title: 3.5 Nitrogen and Sulfur — learner notes
content:
# 3.5 Nitrogen and Sulfur

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Nitrogen and Sulfur — 3.5.1

### Ammonia, ammonium and proton transfer

Ammonia has three N–H bonds and one lone pair on nitrogen. It is a Brønsted–Lowry base because it accepts a proton. Nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+, forming NH4+. The donated pair makes a co-ordinate covalent bond in the formation description; after formation the four N–H bonds in the ammonium ion are equivalent rather than one being a permanently different weak attachment.

The ammonium ion is tetrahedral, with four bonding pairs and no lone pair on its central nitrogen. Its bond angles are approximately 109.5°. Draw brackets and the overall positive charge. Nitrogen has not acquired an extra electron from the proton: H+ contributes no electron, so the new shared pair comes from nitrogen. The valence count in NH4+ is five from nitrogen plus four from hydrogen minus one for the positive charge: eight electrons in four shared pairs. Topic 1.3 explains the electron-pair geometry.

![Generated tetrahedral ammonium representation, with a solid wedge towards and hashed bond away from the viewer](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/c71e6080-83a7-4657-8e8a-586676770f1f.png)

In water, NH3(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq). Only part of the ammonia reacts in the weak-base model, and the hydroxide concentration makes the solution alkaline. Ammonia does not need an OH group in its original composition to act as a base. It accepts a proton from water, leaving OH−.

Adding a strong base to an ammonium salt reverses the proton-transfer role: NH4+(aq) + OH−(aq) → NH3 + H2O(l). Warming can help release NH3 gas from the mixture. For example, NH4Cl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NH3(g) + NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) under the stated warming. Damp red litmus turns blue in a suitable ammonia-gas test. Do not explain this as oxidation of nitrogen: it remains −3 in NH3 and NH4+. The change is transfer of a proton, and the equation gives one mole of ammonia per mole of ammonium ion used.

### Why soils lose nutrient elements

Growing plants take up nutrient elements including nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. When crops are harvested and removed, some of those elements leave the field in the crop material. Repeated farming can therefore deplete an available nutrient supply unless it is replenished. A plant does not create a nutrient element from water simply because its mass increases.

Leaching is a separate loss pathway. Water moving through soil can dissolve and transport nutrient-containing species below the root zone or into drainage. Highly soluble nitrate can move readily in this way. The process depends on water movement, nutrient form, soil retention and plant uptake; a dry period and a heavy-rainfall period need not give equal losses from the same field.

Phosphorus and potassium are also removed by harvest, but their soil species do not necessarily leach as readily as nitrate. Phosphate can interact strongly with soil solids, and potassium can be retained by some soil surfaces. Losses can still occur depending on soil composition, dissolved transport and movement of soil particles. Do not interpret “NPK depletion” as evidence that all three elements have identical water solubility or travel in the same ions.

For an original inventory, a field that loses 20.0 mol of a nutrient in harvested material and 5.00 mol through drainage has lost 25.0 mol through those two measured pathways. That total does not include an unmeasured process automatically. A fertiliser comparison should consider which nutrient is deficient and what reaches the roots, rather than merely choosing the largest product mass. This links the chemistry of soluble species to the soil application without inventing a recommended dose for a particular Namibian farm.

### Abundant nitrogen is not automatically available nitrogen

Nitrogen gas is abundant in air, but the N2 molecule is relatively unreactive under ordinary room-temperature settings. Its atoms are joined by a strong triple covalent bond. Chemical changes that rearrange this stable molecule often face a large activation barrier. The abundance of nitrogen in the atmosphere therefore does not guarantee that a crop can use it directly.

Industrial ammonia manufacture converts nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). A catalyst and suitable temperature and pressure give a useful production rate while recognising the exothermic reaction's equilibrium limit. The purpose of the process here is to convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form that can be used to make fertiliser compounds. Topic 2.3 explains why low temperature favours the equilibrium product but does not by itself give a useful industrial rate.

Ammonia can react with acids to form ammonium salts. For example, 2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4. These products supply chemically accessible nitrogen rather than expecting N2 gas to react readily in the soil by the same uncatalysed industrial pathway. Biological nitrogen fixation can also convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable compounds; the existence of that specialised route does not make ordinary N2 chemically reactive in every setting.

An explanation of fertiliser manufacture should connect bond stability, difficulty of direct reaction and conversion into suitable compounds. Saying “plants need nitrogen” identifies the nutrient role but leaves out why industrial conversion is useful. Saying “nitrogen has a triple bond” names a structure but should also connect it to strong bonding and the reaction barrier. The industrial catalyst changes the pathway and approach rate, while the overall atom balance still requires one N2 for two NH3.

### Tracking nitrogen through different forms

Use the oxidation-number rules from Topic 2.2 to track the specified nitrogen species. In NH3, three hydrogens at +1 require nitrogen −3. In uncombined N2, nitrogen is zero. In NO3−, three oxygens at −2 require nitrogen +5. These values refer to the nitrogen atoms, not the overall charge of each molecule or ion.

For N2O, oxygen contributes −2 and the molecule is neutral. The two nitrogen atoms therefore contribute +2 together, giving an average oxidation number of +1. This average does not claim that the two chemically different positions in the actual molecule must have identical local electronic descriptions. It is the whole-molecule accounting value requested for this comparison.

Fixing N2 into ammonia takes nitrogen from 0 to −3 and is reduction. Conversion of reduced nitrogen into nitrate raises its oxidation number towards +5 and is oxidation. Processes that return nitrate nitrogen to N2 lower the value from +5 towards 0 and are reductions; N2O can occur among gaseous nitrogen-containing forms in the cycle. Different biological and chemical steps carry out the transformations rather than a single universal reaction in one vessel.

Follow the direction before assigning a redox label. NH3 to NO3− is an increase of eight oxidation-number units per nitrogen atom; the reverse change would be a decrease. The atom does not become a new element when its number changes. Nitrogen is conserved even when it moves from dissolved species into a gas that leaves the soil. That phase transfer can remove plant-available nitrogen locally while keeping nitrogen in the wider cycle. Naming the species and calculating their values makes this a chemical account rather than a memorised circular arrow.

### From ammonia to a fertiliser product

Ammonia is important industrially because it is a starting material for nitrogen-containing fertilisers and other nitrogen compounds. Its reaction with an acid can form an ammonium salt. With sulphuric acid, 2NH3 + H2SO4 → (NH4)2SO4; with nitric acid, NH3 + HNO3 → NH4NO3. These acid–base equations show nitrogen entering salts rather than turning N2 directly into a plant nutrient without chemical conversion.

The nitrogen mass percentage depends on the composition. Ammonium sulphate contains two nitrogen atoms per composition unit. With supplied relative atomic masses N 14, H 1, S 32 and O 16, its molar mass is 132 g mol⁻¹ and nitrogen contributes 28 g mol⁻¹. Its nitrogen percentage is 28/132 × 100, about 21.2%. A product's total mass is therefore not the same as its mass of nitrogen.

Ammonium nitrate contains nitrogen in both the ammonium and nitrate parts, with different oxidation numbers. The compound name does not make the two nitrogen environments identical. A mixture described as NPK fertiliser contains nutrient sources for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium; the exact proportions and chemical forms need the supplied composition data.

Industrial importance does not imply that more soluble fertiliser should be added without limit. A useful agricultural supply must match crop demand and soil information, while losses into drainage reduce efficiency. Compare nutrient amount, availability and environmental pathways when data are given. At this level, identify ammonia as a chemical feedstock and explain how its salts can supply accessible nitrogen. Keep the manufacturing reaction separate from the field processes that later release, retain, transform or remove the nutrient.

### Leaching, eutrophication and water quality

A soluble nitrate fertiliser dissolves in soil water and can be taken up by roots. If dissolved nitrate is carried away before uptake, some of the applied nutrient is lost through drainage or runoff. Groundwater can receive that transported nitrate, so a borehole drawing from affected water may contain contamination. The word “borehole” does not itself guarantee that nutrient-rich surface water cannot influence the source.

Nutrient enrichment of a lake or slow-moving water body can stimulate excessive growth of algae or other aquatic producers. As the material dies and is decomposed, microorganisms use dissolved oxygen. Oxygen depletion can harm fish and other organisms. This linked process is eutrophication. State the growth and decomposition stages rather than saying simply that nitrate removes oxygen directly in a one-step reaction.

The outcome depends on nutrient loading, water movement, light and other ecological factors, so a single small addition need not cause the same visible result in every water body. Soluble fertiliser can contribute to the nutrient input without being the only possible source. Compare the transport pathway and amounts in a supplied scenario before assigning a cause to one field.

Nitrate contamination of drinking-water sources is a separate concern from visible algal growth. A clear sample may contain dissolved species that cannot be seen. Chemical measurement is needed to assess the relevant contaminant; appearance or absence of smell is not a concentration result. The syllabus requires recognition of possible contamination, not a diagnosis or an invented safe concentration. A reasoned explanation links high solubility to transport and possible exposure, and links aquatic nutrient enrichment to growth, decay and oxygen use. This supports environmental evaluation of fertiliser use alongside its agricultural benefit.

### Benefits of less immediately soluble nutrient sources

Organic fertilisers such as suitable composted plant or animal material can contain nutrients in forms that are less immediately soluble than a readily soluble nitrate salt. Decomposition and other soil processes progressively release chemically available nutrients. This can spread supply over time rather than placing the entire nutrient amount into soil water at once.

Lower immediate solubility can reduce rapid leaching in a comparison where other relevant factors are suitable. More nutrient may remain in or near the soil until it becomes available for uptake. This can improve retention relative to a soluble application followed immediately by heavy water movement. Explain the benefit through delayed release and transport rather than claiming that an organic label prevents movement of all nutrient species.

Organic materials differ in composition and can also contain soluble nutrient fractions. They may release nutrients when crop demand is low, and runoff or excessive application can still contribute to water pollution. The timing depends on material, soil and environmental settings. A slower-release source can also be less immediately available where a crop needs a prompt supply. These are trade-offs, not reasons to classify either fertiliser type as universally best.

For a supplied choice, compare the same nutrient amount rather than only the same mass of product. A bulky organic material and a concentrated nitrate salt can contain very different nitrogen percentages. Use data on release rate, rainfall or irrigation and uptake where available. State a conditional benefit, such as lower immediate leaching under a particular water regime, and a limitation, such as uncertain timing of release. This connects the solubility argument to the environmental mechanisms above without inventing a field-specific recommendation.

---

## Nitrogen and Sulfur — 3.5.2

### Where sulphur dioxide comes from

Sulphur dioxide is an atmospheric pollutant associated with burning fuels that contain sulphur compounds and with processing sulphide ores. Sulphur in the feed is oxidised during combustion or roasting. The simplified elemental relation is S + O2 → SO2. The sulphur may originally be in a compound, so the fuel is not assumed to contain only free yellow sulphur. Elemental sulphur changes from oxidation number 0 to +4 in SO2, consistent with oxidation and the oxygen consumed in this equation.

Coal and petroleum-derived fuels can contain sulphur-bearing material. If it is oxidised to SO2, increasing the mass of sulphur burned increases the potential gas amount unless capture or another pathway intervenes. Carbon combustion produces carbon oxides, whereas sulphur supplies the sulphur atom of SO2. A fuel's carbon content cannot by itself establish its sulphur dioxide output.

Roasting sulphide ores gives a second source. As the feed is heated in oxygen, sulphur can leave as SO2 while the metal-bearing material changes to a form suitable for further extraction. The precise equation depends on the ore, but the pathway connects to the copper-processing outline in Topic 3.3. Not every ore is a sulphide, so the pollutant cannot be assigned equally to every metal extraction solely from the word mining.

For original amount arithmetic, 1.00 mol of sulphur atoms can give 1.00 mol SO2 in the simplified complete-oxidation model. Using molar masses 32.0 and 64.0 g mol⁻¹, 32.0 g sulphur corresponds to 64.0 g SO2, with oxygen supplying the extra mass. Actual atmospheric release also depends on combustion and capture. Distinguish pollutant formed from pollutant emitted when interpreting an industrial scenario; neither a fuel label nor a reaction equation replaces an emission measurement.

### Breathing effects and acid deposition

Sulphur dioxide is relevant to health because exposure can affect breathing. WHO identifies an association between SO2 exposure and asthma-related hospital and emergency visits. This is a reason to control exposure, not a claim that an observed illness in one person can be diagnosed from a nearby chimney. The chemistry resource concerns the pollutant pathway and general consequence rather than individual medical assessment.

SO2 also contributes to acid rain and other acidic deposition. It dissolves and reacts in atmospheric water, and oxidation can produce sulphuric acid. A simplified overall balance is 2SO2 + O2 + 2H2O → 2H2SO4. The real atmosphere contains several reaction pathways, so this net equation does not describe a single collision occurring as written.

Acidic water can change soil and surface-water chemistry and harm susceptible organisms. It also reacts with carbonate building materials such as limestone: CaCO3 + 2H+ → Ca2+ + CO2 + H2O. The material is gradually lost through chemical reaction, not simply stained by a coloured gas. Nitrogen oxides can contribute to acidic deposition as well, so identifying SO2 as a cause does not mean it is the only atmospheric acid precursor.

When evaluating a proposed control, identify the target. Reducing SO2 formation or capturing it lowers a precursor to both exposure and acid deposition. Filtering dust alone does not establish that SO2 has been removed, and a measured stack concentration does not directly equal the concentration inhaled by a population after dispersion. A complete explanation connects the source, gas transport or chemical transformation, and the named effect. No numerical exposure threshold is needed to recall the syllabus's breathing and acid-rain consequences.

### Low-sulphur fuels and interpreting a guideline

Using a lower-sulphur fuel reduces the sulphur available to form SO2 in a comparable combustion process. This is a source-control approach. Gas treatment can provide an additional control after formation. The relevance to vehicles and power generation follows the same atom balance: less sulphur feed generally means less potential sulphur dioxide, while the actual emitted amount also depends on capture and operation.

For an original comparison, two equal 1000 kg fuel batches containing 1.00% and 0.200% sulphur supply 10.0 kg and 2.00 kg sulphur respectively. Under the simplified complete-conversion model they could form 20.0 kg and 4.00 kg SO2. These are potential formation masses, not measured emissions. The example shows how changing fuel composition can reduce a pollutant source without assigning any current value to a named station.

The syllabus refers to WHO limits in this context. WHO's air-quality guidelines are health-based recommendations for pollutant concentrations over specified exposure averaging periods. They can inform national standards, but do not themselves establish a particular plant's legal emission permit. Keep ambient exposure, stack emissions and legal compliance distinct. This clarification follows the [official WHO explanation](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/who-global-air-quality-guidelines).

Van Eck at Windhoek is the syllabus's named power-station context. A question can use it to ask why low-sulphur fuel helps reduce SO2. A claim that the station currently meets or exceeds a requirement would instead need current relevant measurements, averaging basis and the applicable requirement. No such compliance claim is made from the chemical equation. State the control's purpose and the evidence required to assess it, preserving the syllabus lesson while keeping the meaning of a guideline precise.
