# 4.3 Halogen derivatives

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Halogen derivatives — 4.3.1

### Representing halogenoalkanes

A halogenoalkane, also called a haloalkane, has one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane replaced by halogen atoms. The halogen is bonded to a saturated carbon. Write X as a placeholder for F, Cl, Br or I when discussing the family. A saturated open-chain monohalogenoalkane has general composition CnH2n+1X; if two hydrogens are replaced, the corresponding count is CnH2nX2. Do not apply the monohalogen count to a molecule containing several halogens.

Structural condensed notation CH3CH2Br shows bromoethane's two-carbon connection and terminal bromine. A displayed drawing shows each C–H, C–C and C–Br bond. In skeletal notation the carbon positions and carbon-bound hydrogens can be omitted, but the halogen label must be written. A line ending at a printed Br means a bond to bromine, not an additional carbon hidden under that label.

Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms serve different purposes. A molecular formula gives actual atom counts, an empirical formula gives their simplest ratio, and the remaining forms preserve connectivity with different amounts of detail. For bromoethane, C2H5Br alone does not display each bond. Supplying that count when asked to draw the displayed structure leaves the representation unfinished.

![Original displayed bromoethane](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/e8d3e771-6b11-413b-ad6c-feea6e44824c.png)

Carbon still needs four bond contributions: in CH3CH2Br the first carbon has three H and one C bond; the second has two H, one C and one Br bond. The neutral halogen has one covalent bond in this simple representation. Topic 4.2 supplies the hydrocarbon skeleton conventions, and this topic adds explicit halogen attachments without changing the valency-counting method.

### Naming halogen attachments

Choose the longest suitable carbon chain and name it as the parent alkane. Number the chain to obtain the lowest permitted sequence of substituent locants, comparing the first point of difference. The halogen prefixes are fluoro-, chloro-, bromo- and iodo-. A locant identifies the parent carbon carrying each halogen. Thus CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl is 1-chlorobutane, while CH3CHBrCH3 is 2-bromopropane.

Use di- or tri- when the same halogen appears more than once and give a locant for each occurrence. BrCH2CH2Br is 1,2-dibromoethane. Both numbers matter: 1,1-dibromoethane would put both bromines on one carbon and describe a different connectivity. A number records position, whereas di- records how many substituents of that type are present.

When different halogens occur, write their prefixes in alphabetical order. BrCH2CH2CH2Cl is 1-bromo-3-chloropropane: both numbering directions give the locant set 1,3, and the alphabetically earlier bromo receives the lower locant in this tie. Alphabetical order of prefixes is a writing rule; it does not mean their physical positions must follow that order along a drawing. Ignore multiplicative di- and tri- when ordering different substituent names.

Work backwards to check a proposed name: draw the parent, mark the stated carbon numbers, attach each halogen and complete hydrogen valencies. For 1,2-dibromoethane the two carbons each bear two hydrogens, giving BrCH2CH2Br. If the reconstruction does not match the given connectivity, revisit numbering or parent selection. Parent chains up to six carbons are used here, matching the syllabus naming range. Topic 4.1 introduces the shared stems and naming language.

### Counting halogen and hydrogen separately

Count the carbon skeleton, including branches, and then count every printed halogen label. At each carbon complete four bond contributions with hydrogen. A terminal carbon attached to another carbon and to Br has two hydrogens, not three. A carbon attached to two other carbons and one Br has one hydrogen. The halogen replaces a hydrogen attachment; it is not an extra group added on top of a completed CH3 carbon.

For CH3CHBrCH2Cl, the first carbon supplies three hydrogens, the middle carbon one and the terminal carbon two. The molecular count is C3H6BrCl. An open-chain propane skeleton would have eight hydrogens; replacing two by halogens leaves six, confirming the direct count. The structure is 2-bromo-1-chloropropane after lowest-locant numbering, illustrating that atom counting and naming ask related but distinct questions.

In a skeletal drawing, trace each unlabelled carbon end and vertex once. If a final line meets the printed symbol Cl, that endpoint is chlorine. Inventing an extra carbon there would increase both the carbon and hydrogen totals. Conversely, omitting a labelled halogen from the atom count gives the composition of a different substance even if the carbon count happens to agree.

A molecular formula records actual atom numbers, while an empirical formula records their simplest ratio. Structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms additionally communicate connections. For BrCH2CH2Br, molecular C2H4Br2 reduces to empirical CH2Br; neither request is satisfied by accidentally giving the other. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations should therefore be chosen deliberately. Topic 1.1 explains composition calculations from measurements, whereas the present method reads atoms directly from a supplied structure.

### Substitution and elimination use different routes

Heating bromoethane with aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide gives ethanol by nucleophilic substitution: CH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−. A hydroxide lone pair forms a bond to the electron-deficient carbon attached to Br while the C–Br bond pair goes to Br. Draw a full curved arrow from oxygen's lone pair to that carbon and a second from C–Br to Br. In this direct primary-halogenoalkane route, the changes occur together; there is no separate ethyl carbocation intermediate.

![Original substitution pair arrows](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/b6fbfcca-4cc8-466f-98ba-06c8827f6c40.png)

Heating bromoethane with ethanolic potassium or sodium cyanide gives CH3CH2CN, propanenitrile: CH3CH2Br + CN− → CH3CH2CN + Br−. The attacking carbon of cyanide becomes part of the organic product, so the chain gains one carbon. Heating with excess ethanolic ammonia favours ethanamine: CH3CH2Br + 2NH3 → CH3CH2NH2 + NH4Br. The first attack gives an alkylammonium species; another ammonia removes a proton. Excess ammonia favours attack by ammonia rather than further alkylation of the amine, although it does not guarantee a pure single product.

Heating 2-bromopropane with ethanolic hydroxide instead favours elimination. CH3CHBrCH3 + OH− → CH3CH=CH2 + H2O + Br−. The base removes hydrogen from a neighbouring carbon as the carbon–carbon double bond forms and Br leaves. Hydrogen and bromine are removed from adjacent carbons; they are not replaced by OH on the same carbon. Aqueous hydroxide favours the substitution preparation, while heated ethanolic hydroxide favours this elimination preparation. Carry solvent and heating information with the predicted product. Topic 4.4 studies the resulting alcohol chemistry; Topic 4.2 studies the resulting alkene.

---

## Halogen derivatives — 4.3.2

### Interpreting hydrolysis reactivity

Compare halogenoalkanes with the same carbon skeleton under matched temperature, solvent composition and reagent concentration. Changing several factors at once would make a rate difference ambiguous. For analogous alkyl compounds, hydrolysis tends to become faster in the order fluoroalkane, chloroalkane, bromoalkane, iodoalkane. The C–halogen bond becomes weaker down that sequence, making the required bond breaking easier in the relevant reaction pathway.

The C–F bond is strongly polar because fluorine is much more electronegative than carbon, but it is also particularly strong. A prediction based on polarity alone would therefore be misleading. An iodoalkane can hydrolyse more rapidly than its fluoro analogue despite the C–I bond's smaller polarity. The explanation must consider the energy and pathway for bond cleavage, not just the partial positive charge at carbon.

Suppose equal concentrations of chloroethane, bromoethane and iodoethane are compared in the same solvent at the same temperature. If the measured times to a defined equal extent of reaction are 150 s, 45 s and 12 s, the iodo compound reaches that endpoint fastest. This evidence supports faster hydrolysis under the stated settings; it is not a claim that a reaction time is a universal constant for that compound. Changing the endpoint would change the times used in the comparison.

Keep the carbon skeleton matched because substitution pattern can affect mechanism and rate. The simple halogen trend is not a licence to rank arbitrary primary, secondary and tertiary molecules using just one bond-energy number. Topic 2.4 supplies the broader kinetic reasoning, and the final section here distinguishes bond energy, bond length and polarity as different properties.

### Uses depend on resistance during service

Fluorinated compounds can be relatively resistant to chemical attack because C–F bonds are strong. A molecule that remains stable during use can be useful where unwanted reaction would damage equipment or contaminate a material. Fluorohalogenoalkanes were historically used as refrigerants and aerosol propellants partly because of their relative chemical inertness during normal service. Their physical properties, including suitable volatility, also mattered: bond strength alone does not explain the complete engineering choice.

Relative inertness needs a setting. Resistance to reaction in the lower atmosphere or inside equipment does not mean resistance to energetic ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere. A chlorofluoroalkane can survive long enough to be transported upwards and then undergo photochemical C–Cl cleavage. Its C–F bonds being strong does not prevent a different bond in the molecule from breaking. Treating the molecule as if all its bonds had fluorine's bond strength would miss the ozone problem.

An explanation of a use should connect a material property to the application. For a refrigerant example, stability under ordinary operating settings limits unwanted chemical reaction, while evaporation and condensation transfer thermal energy. It is insufficient to say “it contains fluorine, therefore it is useful” without identifying the relevant property and task. Equally, usefulness in one setting does not establish environmental suitability after release.

The next sections explain the separate ozone consequence and the development of replacement compounds. The discussion is historical and conceptual; it does not claim that a particular substance is currently permitted in a jurisdiction or recommend a refrigerant for a modern installation. Such a choice would require additional engineering and current regulatory information beyond the chemistry comparison taught here.

### Chlorofluoroalkanes and stratospheric ozone

Stratospheric ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation that would otherwise reach Earth's surface in greater amounts. Ozone depletion means a reduction in that protective ozone concentration. Chlorofluoroalkanes, often called CFCs, can be sufficiently persistent in the lower atmosphere to reach the stratosphere. Energetic ultraviolet radiation there can break a C–Cl bond homolytically and release a chlorine radical.

One simplified catalytic cycle is Cl• + O3 → ClO• + O2, followed by ClO• + O → Cl• + O2. Adding the two steps cancels Cl• and ClO• and gives O3 + O → 2O2. Chlorine radical is regenerated, so its effect is not limited to removing one ozone molecule and then becoming permanently used up. This example uses atomic oxygen already present in stratospheric photochemistry; the second step is not a claim that atomic oxygen is the main bulk form of atmospheric oxygen.

The consequence is reduced shielding from harmful ultraviolet radiation. Keep this chain of reasoning distinct from the enhanced greenhouse effect, which concerns absorption of outgoing infrared radiation. The same broad environmental discussion can include both, but they are different mechanisms involving different radiation and atmospheric roles. Ozone also has a different effect near the ground, where it contributes to air pollution; its usefulness in the stratosphere does not make ground-level ozone desirable.

When a compound contains fluorine and chlorine, identify which bond supplies the relevant radical rather than assuming that fluorine is responsible because C–F is polar. The stability of the original molecule during ordinary service can help it reach the region where photolysis occurs. Topic 4.2 provides radical-chain language, while the preceding section shows why an apparently useful property can have a different consequence after environmental release.

### Replacement compounds and ozone recovery

Replacement compounds were developed to preserve useful applications while reducing damage to stratospheric ozone. One structural approach is to avoid chlorine in a refrigerant molecule, so it cannot supply chlorine radicals by C–Cl photolysis. Hydrofluorocarbons contain hydrogen, fluorine and carbon but no chlorine. They illustrate how changing molecular composition can remove the specific chlorine-based ozone-destruction route associated with CFCs.

Some earlier replacement families retained chlorine but incorporated hydrogen, which can make lower-atmosphere breakdown more likely. Such a change can reduce the fraction reaching the stratosphere, but retaining chlorine means the compound should not be described as structurally incapable of releasing chlorine radicals. Distinguish a reduced contribution from complete removal of a proposed source.

Reduced input of ozone-destroying substances allows natural ozone formation and destruction processes to move towards recovery. It does not imply that previously released persistent molecules disappear immediately or that adding a replacement repairs ozone directly. The replacement reduces further damaging input; atmospheric processes then determine the timescale. This explanation does not depend on claiming a current measured size of the ozone hole or forecasting a particular recovery year.

A compound with no chlorine can still absorb infrared radiation and contribute to warming. Evaluating ozone depletion and greenhouse impact therefore requires two separate questions. For example, the structural observation that a candidate refrigerant contains C, H and F but no Cl supports absence of its chlorine-radical source. It supplies no numerical information about atmospheric lifetime or warming effect. A careful conclusion states what the evidence establishes and what additional properties would be needed for a complete comparison, rather than calling a replacement environmentally harmless from one structural feature.

### Energy, length and polarity are different comparisons

Bond energy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in gaseous species; tabulated mean bond energies average over suitable molecular environments. Breaking bonds requires energy. Bond length is the distance between the bonded nuclei at their stable separation, commonly expressed in picometres. Bond polarity is unequal sharing of the bonding electron density because the bonded atoms differ in electronegativity. It is indicated by partial charges, not by assigning complete ionic charges to a neutral covalent molecule.

For comparable carbon–halogen bonds, the halogen atom becomes larger from F to I, so C–halogen length increases. Bond strength generally decreases along C–F, C–Cl, C–Br, C–I. This is a trend within a specified related family, not a universal mathematical rule linking the length of any two unrelated bonds to their reaction rate. Electronic structure and the rest of each molecule also matter.

The halogen attracts the C–halogen pair more strongly than carbon does, leaving carbon δ+ and halogen δ−. A nucleophile can donate a pair to that electron-deficient carbon. However, the particularly strong C–F bond resists breaking even though it is very polar. Thus “more polar” and “more easily hydrolysed” are different judgments and can lead to different rankings.

As a worked interpretation, suppose analogous compounds have supplied C–X breaking energies 340 and 240 kJ mol−1. The lower value represents easier isolated gaseous bond breaking, but neither number alone specifies the whole activation barrier in solution. Use it alongside the matched hydrolysis evidence and settings. Topic 1.3 explains electronegativity and bond polarity, Topic 2.1 uses bond energies in overall enthalpy estimates, and Topic 2.4 distinguishes those estimates from the kinetic barrier determining rate.

# 4.3 Halogen derivatives — practice tasks and worked answers



## ITEM-8224-4.3-P01

6 marks · Bloom: Apply

Identify the correct option in each question (1 mark each).
1. Name CH3CH2CH2Cl. A 1-chloropropane; B 2-chloropropane; C 1-chlorobutane; D propene
2. Identify the gas region protected by ozone relevant to CFC depletion. A ground-level smog; B stratospheric ozone layer; C dissolved oxygen in water; D a fuel tank
3. Identify a structural approach removing a refrigerant chlorine-radical source. A increase chlorine content; B ignore structure; C use a suitable chlorine-free replacement; D make more CFC
4. Name CH3CHBrCH2CH3. A 1-bromobutane; B 3-bromobutane; C 2-bromopropane; D 2-bromobutane
5. Identify the supported conclusion if a CFC radical is regenerated in an ozone cycle. A it can react repeatedly; B it is permanently consumed in the first step; C it becomes a harmless final polymer; D ozone is unaffected
6. Identify the supported conclusion for a replacement containing C,H,F but no Cl. A it cannot warm the atmosphere; B it lacks a C–Cl chlorine source; C it instantly repairs existing ozone loss; D its lifetime is known numerically



### Worked answer

1. Key/correct option A. A matches three carbons and terminal Cl; B moves Cl, C adds carbon and D removes halogen and changes bonding. Each distractor reflects the specified error.
2. Key/correct option B. B is the protective ozone layer; A is a different ozone problem and C/D are unrelated locations. Each distractor reflects the specified error.
3. Key/correct option C. C removes its C–Cl source; A/D retain or increase that source and B supplies no chemical solution. Each distractor reflects the specified error.
4. Key/correct option D. D gives the correct four-carbon parent and lower locant; A moves Br, B misnumbers, C loses carbon. Each distractor reflects the specified error.
5. Key/correct option A. A follows regeneration; B contradicts it, C invents a product and D ignores net ozone loss. Each distractor reflects the specified error.
6. Key/correct option B. B follows composition; A/C overstate consequences and D requires measurements not given. Each distractor reflects the specified error.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: key, correct option, distractor, error. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-4.3-P02

8 marks · Bloom: Apply

Explain changes to a two-carbon saturated molecule bearing one Br.
(a) Draw its displayed structure and name it. [3]
(b) State its molecular composition. [1]
(c) Write its ionic reaction with heated aqueous hydroxide. [2]
(d) Explain why heated ethanolic cyanide gives a three-carbon organic product. [2]



### Worked answer

(a) Two single-bonded C atoms [1], three H on one and two H plus Br on the other [1], bromoethane [1]. (b) C2H5Br [1]. (c) CH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br−: organic change [1], correct ionic balance [1]. (d) Carbon of CN− bonds to the carbon losing Br [1]; its added carbon gives CH3CH2CN, propanenitrile [1]. Creditworthy points shown per part, total8 marks.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: part, mark, creditworthy point. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-4.3-P03

5 marks · Bloom: Apply

Calculate the maximum ethanol mass obtainable by complete hydrolysis of 5.45 g of the saturated two-carbon monobromo compound. Name and represent that reactant. Use Ar(C)=12.0, Ar(H)=1.0, Ar(Br)=79.9 and Mr(ethanol)=46.0. [5]



### Worked answer

Bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, molecular composition C2H5Br [1]. Equation: CH3CH2Br + OH− → CH3CH2OH + Br− [1], so mole ratio1:1. Working: Mr(bromoethane)=2(12.0)+5(1.0)+79.9=108.9; n=5.45/108.9=0.0500459 mol [1]. Ethanol n=0.0500459 mol [1]; m=0.0500459×46.0=2.30211 g, answer2.30 g to three significant figures [1]. Mass units already g; retain unrounded intermediate values.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: equation, working, answer, unit, significant figures. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.

# 4.4 Hydroxyl compounds

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Hydroxyl compounds — 4.4.1

### Representing the alcohol families

An alcohol has a hydroxyl group, –OH, attached to a saturated carbon. For an open-chain saturated molecule with one hydroxyl group and no other functional group, the general composition is CnH2n+2O, also written CnH2n+1OH. The hydrogen on oxygen is part of the total hydrogen count. This relationship does not apply without qualification to molecules containing rings, additional multiple bonds or several hydroxyl groups.

Structural condensed notation CH3CH2OH makes ethanol's connections clear: two carbon atoms lead to O–H. A displayed drawing must show the C–O and O–H bonds, together with each C–H bond. In skeletal notation the carbon skeleton can omit carbon-bound hydrogen, but O and its attached H must remain explicit. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms answer different requests: a molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio, and the other forms retain connectivity.

![Original displayed ethanol with explicit O–H](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/b50c0979-26fa-49ca-8f9f-05380fe71767.png)

The local environment of the carbon bearing OH distinguishes alcohol classes. CH3CH2OH is primary because that carbon has one carbon neighbour. CH3CH(OH)CH3 is secondary because it has two, while (CH3)3COH is tertiary because it has three. The oxygen has one bond to carbon and one to hydrogen in each example; classifying by oxygen's two bonds would not distinguish them.

Keep branches and OH on their specified atoms when converting representations. In the tertiary example the central carbon has no attached H: it is bonded to three methyl carbons and oxygen. Drawing an additional H there would give five single bonds. Topic 4.1 supplies representation conventions, while the classification section below connects the OH-bearing carbon's attachments to oxidation behaviour.

### Naming the hydroxyl position

Choose the longest suitable chain containing the carbon attached to OH and use the ending –ol. Number from the end giving the hydroxyl group its lowest permitted locant. The one-to-six-carbon parent stems are meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent- and hex-. Methanol and ethanol have no distinct alternative hydroxyl position after equivalent end numbering. Longer chains can require a number: CH3CH2CH2OH is propan-1-ol and CH3CH(OH)CH3 is propan-2-ol.

The locant belongs immediately before –ol in the naming style used here. For CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3, start numbering from the end nearer OH and obtain butan-2-ol. Butan-3-ol would describe the same connections with unnecessarily high numbering. Position is read from the molecular connections, not from which end happens to be printed on the left.

Branches are included as prefixes with their own locants. (CH3)2CHCH2OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol: a three-carbon parent includes the OH-bearing carbon, and carbon 2 has a methyl substituent. (CH3)3COH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Both contain four carbons altogether but differ in the OH-bearing carbon's attachments. The names distinguish those connections instead of merely announcing a total atom count.

To check a name, draw the numbered parent, attach OH at the stated carbon and add the substituents. Complete valencies last, including O–H. Reconstructing propan-2-ol gives one hydrogen on the OH-bearing carbon, whereas reconstructing 2-methylpropan-2-ol gives none there. Naming and classification thus provide useful independent checks, but neither replaces the requested drawing or molecular count when a question asks for those forms. Topic 4.2 uses related locant reasoning for carbon–carbon double bonds.

### Counting atoms without losing the OH hydrogen

Count all carbon atoms, including methyl branches, then count oxygen and hydrogen separately. Carbon has four bond contributions; neutral alcohol oxygen has two single bonds, normally one to carbon and one to hydrogen. The hydrogen in OH can be overlooked when expanding a skeletal drawing, so include it explicitly in the final total. Classifying a molecule as primary, secondary or tertiary does not change this accounting method.

For CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, two CH3 groups supply six hydrogen atoms, the OH-bearing CH supplies one, CH2 supplies two and OH supplies one. The total is ten, giving C4H10O. For (CH3)3COH, three methyl groups supply nine hydrogens and OH supplies one; the central carbon supplies none. The result is also C4H10O. Equal composition therefore does not prove equal connectivity or equal alcohol class.

For a saturated open-chain alcohol with one OH, use CnH2n+2O as a check after reading the structure. With n=4 it predicts H10, matching both examples. This check cannot locate OH or distinguish a branched structure from an unbranched one. It is also not a replacement for reading additional functional groups if the given molecule contains them.

A molecular formula states the actual numbers, while an empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio. Structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms show connections in different detail. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal answers are therefore not interchangeable. In ethanol the molecular count C2H6O cannot be reduced further; this coincidence does not make the two definitions identical. Topic 1.1 develops composition from mass data. Here the evidence is the supplied connectivity, and a correct answer follows from completing each atom's allowed bonding.

### Ethanol as a reaction hub

Complete combustion is CH3CH2OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(g) for hot gaseous water. Ethanol can therefore act as a fuel. In substitution with hydrogen bromide under suitable heated acidic settings, CH3CH2OH + HBr → CH3CH2Br + H2O. The OH-derived group is replaced by bromine; this differs from replacing the hydrogen on oxygen in the reaction with sodium.

With sodium, 2CH3CH2OH + 2Na → 2CH3CH2O−Na+ + H2. The product is sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas. The carbon skeleton and C–O connection remain, while the O–H hydrogen is removed. The whole molecule does not become a sodium atom with an attached hydrocarbon, and OH− is not the stated organic product.

Warm acidified dichromate(VI) oxidises ethanol. Controlled oxidation with removal of volatile ethanal as it forms gives CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O. Heating under reflux with excess oxidant permits further oxidation: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O. Acidified dichromate changes from orange towards green as it is reduced. Distillation removes the aldehyde; reflux returns volatile material so reaction can continue. The choice changes the intended organic endpoint.

Dehydration eliminates water to give ethene: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O. Heating with concentrated sulfuric acid, around 170°C for this conventional preparation, supplies a suitable dehydration setting. Passing ethanol vapour over heated aluminium oxide is an alternative catalytic route. Merely naming dilute acid does not specify the concentrated-acid dehydration preparation. The concentration and heating distinguish the stated route from mixing ethanol with a dilute aqueous acid.

Esterification with ethanoic acid gives CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH ⇌ CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O using an acid catalyst and heating. The ester is ethyl ethanoate. At fixed temperature, equilibrium means the reaction need not consume all starting material. Topic 4.7 develops ester structure and hydrolysis; here recognise the alcohol's role and preserve the balance in each reaction.

For a stoichiometric example, the sodium equation shows that 0.200 mol ethanol produces at most 0.100 mol hydrogen when sodium is in excess and reaction is complete. Divide the alcohol amount by two because two O–H hydrogens combine to make each H2 molecule. The ratio follows the balanced equation, not the number of carbon atoms.

### Classifying the carbon carrying OH

Locate OH, then identify the carbon directly bonded to its oxygen. Count the carbon atoms directly attached to that carbon. One gives a primary alcohol, two a secondary alcohol and three a tertiary alcohol. This is a local count. The total length of the molecule and the number of hydrogens elsewhere in the chain do not determine the class. Methanol has no attached carbon group but is conventionally treated with primary alcohols for its oxidation behaviour.

In CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, the OH-bearing carbon is at an end and touches one other carbon, so butan-1-ol is primary. In CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, that carbon touches two carbons, making butan-2-ol secondary. In (CH3)3COH, it touches three methyl carbons, making 2-methylpropan-2-ol tertiary. All three examples contain one OH group; “tertiary” does not mean three hydroxyl groups.

The same local count shows how much hydrogen is attached to the OH-bearing carbon. A usual primary RCH2OH has two, a secondary R2CHOH has one, and a tertiary R3COH has none. These patterns help explain the simple oxidation outcomes: forming a carbonyl by removal of the O–H hydrogen and a hydrogen on the same carbon is possible for the first two types. The tertiary type lacks that second hydrogen.

Practise circling the relevant carbon before assigning a class, particularly in branched structures. For (CH3)2CHCH2OH the branched carbon is not the OH-bearing carbon; the terminal CH2OH still makes it primary. This prevents a neighbouring branch from being mistaken for a tertiary alcohol centre. The next section applies the classification to distinguishing reactions, while Topic 4.6 develops the carbonyl products formed by oxidation.

### Distinguishing alcohols by oxidation

Warm a suitable alcohol with acidified dichromate(VI) in the school oxidation comparison. Primary and secondary alcohols reduce the oxidant as they are oxidised, so an orange-to-green change supports reaction. A tertiary alcohol normally does not undergo the corresponding mild oxidation because its OH-bearing carbon lacks hydrogen. This is a statement about the specified mild route, rather than a claim that severe oxidation could not break other bonds.

A primary alcohol can give an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. For propan-1-ol, controlled oxidation produces propanal, CH3CH2CHO; further oxidation produces propanoic acid. Propan-2-ol gives propanone, CH3COCH3. Keeping the carbon skeleton intact provides a useful check on the oxidation products. An unexpected extra carbon in a proposed product would require an additional reagent or reaction not supplied here.

Suppose samples A and B both change orange dichromate to green, while C does not under matched mild settings. This supports reactive primary or secondary structures for A and B and, among the stated alcohol candidates, a tertiary structure for C. It does not decide which of A and B is primary, because both types react. Additional identification of an aldehyde versus ketone product is required. Topic 4.6 develops the structures of those carbonyl products.

State an observation separately from a conclusion. “Orange becomes green” is observable; “it is secondary” is a structural inference that needs adequate discrimination. To compare samples, match temperature, reagent concentration and observation time. A negative result from a cold mixture or insufficient mixing cannot be treated as an equally controlled comparison. The best distinguishing reaction is one whose different outcomes separate the actual candidate structures given, rather than a memorised colour change applied without checking what it distinguishes.

### The alkaline iodine test identifies a local arrangement

An alcohol containing CH3CH(OH)R can be oxidised under the alkaline iodine test to a methyl carbonyl arrangement and then form triiodomethane, CHI3. The positive observation is a yellow precipitate, not merely disappearance of iodine colour or a yellow solution. Triiodomethane is also called iodoform. Write its identity clearly: three iodines and one hydrogen are attached to its single carbon.

Propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, and butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, have the required local arrangement and give positive results with warm alkaline aqueous iodine. Ethanol also gives the test: it is oxidised to ethanal, which has the required CH3CO– arrangement for the subsequent reaction. This special primary alcohol must not be rejected simply because the other familiar positive alcohol examples are secondary.

Pentan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3, is secondary but lacks a methyl group directly attached to its OH-bearing carbon, so it does not give the corresponding positive alcohol test. Likewise, primary propan-1-ol lacks the required arrangement. Thus a positive result is not a general test for alcohols or even for all secondary alcohols. Inspect the local connections around OH rather than counting methyl groups somewhere else in the molecule.

For an original discrimination, a four-carbon alcohol gives a yellow CHI3 precipitate and is known to be secondary. Butan-2-ol fits both pieces of evidence. The test alone would not have established a unique structure without those restrictions. Nor is the precipitate 2-iodobutane: the alcohol's entire chain has not simply had OH replaced by I. Topic 4.6 connects the test with carbonyl structure. Record reagent, warmth, the solid observation and its chemical identity before drawing the structural conclusion.

### Why alcohols can act as solvents

An alcohol combines a polar hydroxyl group with a hydrocarbon group. Its OH can form hydrogen bonds with water and compatible solutes, while its carbon-containing part provides interactions with less polar substances. This combination allows suitable alcohols to dissolve a range of materials that would not all dissolve equally well in water alone. Dissolution is explained through favourable solute–solvent interactions, not by assuming the alcohol chemically destroys each dissolved substance.

Short-chain alcohols have a relatively large polar contribution and mix well with water. As the hydrocarbon portion becomes larger, its non-polar character becomes more influential and water solubility generally decreases within comparable alcohols. Consequently “contains OH” does not establish unlimited miscibility for an arbitrary long-chain alcohol. Both the molecule's structure and the identity of the solute need consideration.

In cosmetics, a suitable alcohol can help dissolve selected ingredients and distribute them through a formulation; volatility can also assist drying after application. This explains a solvent role and does not assert that all alcohols are appropriate for skin products. In the syllabus's coal application, an alcohol-based solvent can extract compatible soluble sulfur-containing compounds into the solvent phase. Extraction transfers those compounds for later separation. It does not mean that all forms of sulfur, including insoluble mineral material, are removed just by dissolving coal in any alcohol.

Suppose an invented materials laboratory observes that a selected sulfur-containing organic solute dissolves in its chosen alcohol but poorly in water. The supported explanation invokes the balance of polar and hydrocarbon interactions. The observation supplies no percentage removal for a whole coal sample, because that sample may contain other sulfur forms and an inaccessible solid matrix. Topic 1.3 explains hydrogen bonding; Topic 4.3 distinguishes chemical substitution from the physical separation involved here. A useful solvent claim names what is dissolved and the setting in which the solvent works.

# 4.5 Isomerism: structural and stereoisomerism

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Isomerism: structural and stereoisomerism — 4.5

### Enumerating structures systematically

Begin with the molecular composition and any class restriction in the question. The same atom count can sometimes describe several families, so “all isomers” needs the stated scope. A molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio; structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms reveal connectivity. Keep these molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations distinct while checking that a proposed drawing has the required atom count.

For C4H10 as an open-chain alkane, arrange four carbons first in an unbranched route and then in a branched skeleton. The distinct possibilities are butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, and 2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CH. Fill hydrogens to valency four. Drawing butane in a different zigzag or reversing its left-to-right order does not create another connectivity. The two names make it easier to detect duplicate drawings.

For C4H8 restricted to open-chain alkenes with one double bond, use an unbranched four-carbon skeleton and move C=C between inequivalent positions. This gives but-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH3, and but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. Putting the bond at the opposite terminal end repeats but-1-ene. A branched skeleton supplies 2-methylpropene, CH2=C(CH3)2. These are three structural connectivities. Saturated rings are outside this particular question's stated open-chain restriction, rather than being impossible with C4H8.

Now inspect each connectivity for spatial alternatives. But-2-ene has cis and trans forms; the other two have a double-bond carbon with identical attachments and do not give this pair. Thus there are four distinct alkene forms when those two are counted separately. Record whether your total counts connectivities or includes stereoisomers. Check atom numbers, valencies, parent names and duplication at each stage. Topic 4.2 provides naming and composition tools; the later sections here explain the spatial test used in this enumeration.

### Three kinds of structural isomerism

Structural isomers have the same molecular composition but a different arrangement of connections between atoms. Chain isomerism changes the carbon skeleton. Butane and 2-methylpropane both contain four carbons and ten hydrogens, but the first has an unbranched route and the second a carbon attached to three methyl groups. Their difference is not merely that one drawing looks straighter on a page.

Positional isomerism keeps the basic carbon skeleton and functional-group type but changes the position of a group or multiple bond. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol both have three-carbon chains and one OH, but OH is attached at an end in one and at the middle carbon in the other. But-1-ene and but-2-ene supply the corresponding double-bond example. Both members of each pair have matching total atom counts.

Functional-group isomerism changes the functional group while retaining total composition. Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and methoxymethane, CH3OCH3, both have C2H6O. One has an O–H bond as an alcohol; the other has C–O–C connectivity as an ether. This example identifies a family difference; it does not require learning an extra ether reaction scheme. The oxygen's position among the connections supplies the distinguishing evidence.

To assign a type, compare the carbon skeleton, then the functional group and its position. A change in the way a molecule is oriented in space without changing which atoms bond belongs to another comparison. Turning a sheet upside down or rotating a flexible single bond can produce a different-looking sketch of the same compound. Name both drawings and trace each atom's neighbours before counting them separately. A matching molecular atom count is necessary for an isomer pair, but is insufficient: two identical drawings after reorientation also have matching counts. Topic 4.1's functional-group vocabulary helps identify what has actually changed.

For a final duplicate check, label the carbon atoms temporarily and follow the route between branch points or functional groups. Two sketches that can be matched atom for atom with the same neighbours represent one connectivity, even if one has been bent on the page. Remove the temporary labels before giving the chemical structure. By contrast, moving OH from an end carbon to an internal carbon changes its neighbours and gives a positional pair. This method keeps visual appearance separate from the evidence used to classify the isomers.

### Same connections, different arrangement in space

Stereoisomers have the same structural connections but a different arrangement of atoms in space. They also have the same molecular composition. The two divisions used here are geometrical, or cis–trans, isomerism and optical isomerism. A spatial difference must survive attempts to rotate the entire molecule into coincidence; a different viewing angle is not by itself a new stereoisomer.

In but-2-ene the two methyl groups can lie on the same side of C=C or opposite sides. Both structures have the same sequence CH3–CH=CH–CH3. Nothing has been moved from one carbon to another, so this is not positional isomerism. They differ in the arrangement held by the double bond: cis has the methyl groups on the same side and trans has them on opposite sides.

![Original cis and trans but-2-ene drawings](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/5671ac3d-365f-4741-9572-23e5f8031600.png)

Optical isomers in the simple one-centre examples are a pair of non-superimposable mirror images, called enantiomers. A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups provides a common source. A pure member can rotate the plane of plane-polarised light; the corresponding pure mirror form rotates it equally in the opposite direction under matched settings. Equal amounts of the two can cancel the net rotation. This cancellation concerns the sample, not disappearance of the chiral centres in its molecules.

The diagnostic questions differ. For cis–trans, inspect C=C and compare attachments at each end. For the optical examples, inspect a tetrahedral centre and compare its four groups. Do not label any two differently drawn molecules “optical” merely because they have the same counts. Likewise, a cis–trans pair is not automatically a mirror-image pair. The following sections develop the restricted-rotation and four-different-groups tests without adding a new stereochemical naming system.

### Restricted rotation makes cis and trans distinct

A carbon–carbon double bond prevents the free rotation characteristic of a simple carbon–carbon single bond. Twisting the two alkene ends relative to one another would disrupt the π bonding interaction and requires a substantial energy input. Under ordinary settings the cis and trans structures therefore remain distinct rather than continuously exchanging through easy rotation about intact C=C.

Restriction alone is not enough to give two distinguishable forms. Each double-bond carbon must have two different attached groups. But-2-ene meets that test: each carbon has H and CH3. The methyl groups can be on the same side, cis, or opposite sides, trans. In propene, one double-bond carbon has two H atoms. Interchanging those identical hydrogens gives the same arrangement, so propene does not form a cis/trans pair. Likewise CH2=C(CH3)2 fails the test at its CH2 end and at its two-methyl end.

When drawing the but-2-ene pair, put C=C horizontally, give each carbon one H and one CH3, and keep three bonding directions around each alkene carbon. In the cis drawing both methyl labels are above, or both below, the double bond. In trans one is above and the other below. Reversing the entire drawing does not convert cis to trans, because the same-side or opposite-side relationship is unchanged.

Avoid saying simply that cis–trans is caused by molecules being unable to move. Molecules can translate, rotate as whole objects and rotate around other bonds; the relevant constraint is relative rotation about the double bond. That is why a freely rotating butane sketch does not supply an analogous isolable pair just by showing its methyl groups in two positions on paper. Topic 4.1 describes local planar alkene geometry, and Topic 4.2 supplies the names used to identify which bond is under discussion.

### A tetrahedral centre with four different groups

A chiral centre in the carbon examples taught here is a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups. The groups need not begin with four different elements: two can both begin with carbon but differ farther along their connections. For butan-2-ol, the OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, CH3 and CH2CH3. These are four different groups, making that carbon a chiral centre.

Its mirror image has the same atom connections but cannot be placed on the original so that all four groups coincide by rotating the whole molecule. A simple pair of such non-superimposable mirror images gives optical isomerism. A wedge represents a bond towards the viewer, a hashed bond one away, and ordinary lines bonds in the page. A flat four-arm cross without a depth convention does not demonstrate the tetrahedral mirror relationship adequately.

![Original mirror-image butan-2-ol centres](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/5a6ac464-64b5-4cd9-98cc-4be7dfaab4ee.png)

Propan-2-ol does not have this centre because its OH-bearing carbon has two identical methyl groups. A CH2 carbon also has two identical H atoms. Neither becomes chiral simply because the other two groups look different. In a candidate with a longer branch, trace each attached group far enough to decide whether it is genuinely different. The plus or minus sign for measured light rotation cannot be assigned from a wedge drawing by guessing which group lies to the right.

Some molecules contain more than one chiral centre. Identify each candidate locally by its four attachments, but do not assume that the count of centres alone completely describes the whole molecule's optical behaviour. The syllabus does not require a fuller multi-centre classification. The essential transfer here is to inspect actual connections and show depth correctly in a one-centre pair. Topic 4.4 supplies the alcohol structures used in these examples; the centre remains a geometric property rather than a separate alcohol reaction.

### Applying both structural tests

Use two separate inspection routes on a supplied structure. First mark each C=C and inspect the two groups attached at each end. If either end has identical groups, the simple geometrical pair is absent at that bond. If both ends have different groups, the relevant same-side and opposite-side arrangements can be considered where the cis/trans description is unambiguous. Do not infer this property merely from the appearance of two parallel bond lines.

Second inspect tetrahedral carbons. A carbon carrying two H atoms fails the four-different-groups test immediately. A carbon with four different attachments is a candidate chiral centre; mark that atom with an asterisk and identify the groups. The alkene carbons themselves have three attachment directions and are not the tetrahedral centres in this test. Thus the presence of a double bond does not automatically establish a chiral carbon.

For CH3CH=CHCH(OH)CH2CH3, the C=C carbons each have one H and one different carbon-containing group, so geometrical alternatives are possible. The OH-bearing carbon has H, OH, an ethyl group and an unsaturated three-carbon group. Those attachments are different, making it a chiral centre. The example illustrates that both kinds of structural feature can occur in one molecule without requiring a complete catalogue of its spatial forms.

By contrast, CH2=CHCH2OH has a terminal CH2 at the double bond and a CH2OH carbon. It fails the geometrical test because one alkene end has two H, and it fails the tetrahedral test because the alcohol carbon also has two H. State the specific duplicated group when rejecting a candidate. This is more informative than saying that the molecule is “too small” or “not symmetrical enough”. Throughout, preserve atom connections before discussing space: a change in OH position or carbon skeleton would create a structural comparison rather than a different arrangement of the same connections.

# 4.6 Carbonyl compounds

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Carbonyl compounds — 4.6.1

### Aldehyde and ketone connections

A carbonyl group is C=O. In an aldehyde its carbon has at least one attached hydrogen, giving the group –CHO at the end of an open chain. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon groups, giving –CO– within a carbon skeleton. Methanal, HCHO, is the simplest aldehyde and has two H attached to the carbonyl carbon; a ketone needs at least three carbons to provide its two carbon attachments.

For saturated open-chain molecules containing one carbonyl and no other functional group, the general composition is CnH2nO. Propanal, CH3CH2CHO, and propanone, CH3COCH3, both have C3H6O. The count therefore does not decide whether the compound is an aldehyde or ketone. Connectivity supplies that distinction.

Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms describe different information. A molecular formula gives actual counts and an empirical formula their simplest ratio. Structural condensed notation retains grouped connections; a displayed drawing shows each bond; skeletal notation omits carbon labels and their hydrogen while retaining the oxygen and C=O double line. In condensed –CHO, the H is attached to carbon, not to oxygen. Do not read CHO as an alcohol OH group.

![Original aldehyde and ketone carbonyl connections](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/d7fad3a1-274f-44f2-b77d-510a7d233123.png)

Each carbonyl carbon has four bond contributions: two to oxygen and two single-bond attachments. The oxygen has its double bond and no implied O–H hydrogen. Check these details when expanding a skeletal representation. Topic 4.1 explains planar geometry at a carbonyl carbon and infrared carbonyl absorption; Topic 4.4 distinguishes the alcohol C–OH arrangement from the oxidised C=O arrangement.

### Names include the carbonyl carbon

Aldehydes use the ending –al. Select a parent chain containing the CHO carbon and include that carbon in the chain count. It is carbon 1, so CH3CH2CHO is propanal, not ethanal with an extra unnamed group. The one-to-six-carbon straight-chain aldehydes are methanal, ethanal, propanal, butanal, pentanal and hexanal. Branch locants are counted from the aldehyde end.

For example, CH3CH(CH3)CHO is 2-methylpropanal. Its parent has three carbons including CHO, while the methyl substituent adds a fourth to the whole molecule. Reconstructing the name gives the same carbon skeleton and ensures that an H remains attached to the carbonyl carbon. Merely naming the longest chain anywhere in a branched drawing can be wrong if that route omits the aldehyde group.

Ketones use –one and number the parent from the end giving the carbonyl carbon its lowest permitted locant. CH3COCH2CH2CH3 is pentan-2-one. CH3CH2COCH2CH3 is pentan-3-one. Both parents contain five carbons; the number identifies which carbon bears =O. In propanone there is one possible internal carbonyl position, so its usual simple name needs no locant.

To reverse a ketone name, draw the complete parent carbon chain first, number it and add a double bond to oxygen at the named carbon. Then fill the remaining carbon valencies with hydrogen. A terminal carbon bearing =O and H would instead give an aldehyde structure. Naming is therefore tied to connections, rather than a choice of ending based solely on a total atom count. Topic 4.5 uses this difference when identifying functional-group structural isomers.

### Composition from a carbonyl drawing

Count the carbonyl carbon as part of the carbon skeleton, then complete valencies at each carbon. Its double bond to O uses two contributions. In an aldehyde, one remaining contribution can be C–H and the other C–C; in a ketone both remaining contributions are C–C. Oxygen does not carry an implicit hydrogen in C=O. This is a common difference from the alcohol structures used earlier.

For CH3CH2CH2CHO, the hydrogen total is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8, so butanal has C4H8O. For CH3COCH2CH3, the methyl groups supply six H, CH2 supplies two and the carbonyl carbon none, again giving C4H8O. Thus the same count can belong to an aldehyde or a ketone. The molecular composition does not establish the name or structure without further evidence.

In a skeletal drawing, a line to an explicit oxygen label is not an extra carbon position. The two lines of C=O represent a double bond between one carbon and one oxygen, not two oxygen atoms. Counting line strokes instead of labelled atoms and carbon positions would therefore give an impossible composition.

Use the saturated open-chain CnH2nO relationship as a check after the direct count. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms are separate answers: a molecular formula gives actual counts, an empirical formula a ratio, and the connection representations show where atoms attach. Topic 1.1 covers calculating relative molecular mass from those counts. Here a calculated Mr can confirm arithmetic but cannot distinguish two isomers with equal composition.

### Preparing carbonyls from alcohols

Use acidified dichromate(VI), Cr2O7²−/H+, to oxidise primary and secondary alcohols. Ethanol gives ethanal in controlled oxidation: CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O. The primary alcohol loses hydrogen from OH and from the same carbon to form C=O. Further oxidation can produce ethanoic acid, so limiting the intended stage and removing the volatile aldehyde as it forms helps obtain the aldehyde product.

A secondary alcohol instead gives a ketone. Propan-2-ol gives propanone: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O. Its OH-bearing carbon has one H available for removal and two carbon attachments. The product retains those two attachments at the carbonyl carbon. Oxidation of butan-2-ol similarly gives butan-2-one, preserving four carbons and the carbonyl position corresponding to the original OH-bearing carbon.

The oxidant's orange colour changes towards green as dichromate(VI) is reduced. That observation supports oxidation but does not on its own identify which carbonyl formed, since both primary and secondary alcohols can react. Use the starting alcohol's connections and product structure as well. A tertiary alcohol lacks H on its OH-bearing carbon and resists this ordinary mild carbonyl-forming route.

For a worked amount calculation, 0.100 mol propan-2-ol can give at most 0.100 mol propanone if oxidation is complete: the organic ratio is 1:1. Mr(propanone)=3(12.0)+6(1.0)+16.0=58.0, so the corresponding mass is 5.80 g. Actual isolated yield can be lower through incomplete reaction or loss during separation; neither changes the stoichiometric maximum calculated from the balanced equation. Topic 4.4 teaches the alcohol reaction map, and Topic 4.7 develops the carboxylic-acid endpoint of further primary oxidation.

### Worked answer

Propanone, CH3C(=O)CH3, C3H6O [1]. Equation: CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O [1]. Working: n(alcohol)=3.00/60.0=0.0500 mol [1]; ratio1:1 gives0.0500 mol product and Mr=58.0 [1]; m=0.0500×58.0=2.90 g [1]. Answer to three significant figures; masses already g so no prefix conversion needed. This is a theoretical maximum, not an observed isolated yield.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: equation, working, answer, unit, significant figures. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.

title: 4.7 Carboxylic acids and derivatives — learner notes
content:
# 4.7 Carboxylic acids and derivatives

*nam-8224-nsscas-2026. Offline study notes, rendered from the approved content units on 2026-10-22. Everything here is also what the flashcards are built from.*

---

## Carboxylic acids and derivatives — 4.7.1

### Reading the carboxyl group

A carboxylic acid contains the carboxyl group, –C(=O)OH. One oxygen is double-bonded to carbon and the other is single-bonded to that same carbon and to H. The carbon therefore has four bond contributions: two to carbonyl oxygen, one to hydroxyl oxygen and one to its remaining attachment. In methanoic acid the remaining attachment is H; in ethanoic acid it is CH3.

The saturated open-chain monocarboxylic acids with no other functional group follow CnH2nO2. The count n includes the carboxyl carbon. CH3COOH, ethanoic acid, has two carbons altogether, not a two-carbon alkyl group plus an extra carboxyl carbon. In structural condensed notation COOH groups the two oxygens clearly, but a displayed drawing must show C=O, C–O and O–H as separate bonds.

Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms convey different information. A molecular formula gives actual atom counts, an empirical formula their simplest ratio, and the connection forms retain bonding detail. For ethanoic acid these counts are molecular C2H4O2 and empirical CH2O. In a skeletal structure both oxygen labels and the OH hydrogen must be shown; an unlabelled line end is otherwise interpreted as carbon.

![Original acid, ester and primary amine connection patterns](https://storage.googleapis.com/yyenichat_notes_audios_images/Images/afd49c61-cc93-4841-a229-5df600c43447.png)

The OH in COOH is part of a carboxyl group, not a separate alcohol functional group on a saturated carbon. Likewise the C=O here does not make the whole compound an aldehyde or ketone, because its other attachment includes oxygen. Functional-group classification depends on the complete local arrangement. Topic 4.6 explains aldehyde and ketone connections, and this distinction prevents applying their names to a carboxylic acid merely because all contain C=O.

### Naming from the acid end

Replace the parent alkane ending with –oic acid and include the COOH carbon in the parent. The straight-chain one-to-six-carbon members are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid, butanoic acid, pentanoic acid and hexanoic acid. The carboxyl carbon is carbon 1 in these open-chain names. Do not number from the opposite hydrocarbon end just because that end is printed on the left.

CH3CH2CH2COOH has a four-carbon parent, including COOH, and is butanoic acid. CH3CH(CH3)COOH is 2-methylpropanoic acid: its parent route has three carbons and its branch supplies another. The whole molecule still has four carbons. Calling it methylbutanoic acid would imply a longer parent and a different atom count.

To construct a named acid, draw the parent chain with its first carbon as C(=O)OH. Attach branches at the stated numbered positions and complete the remaining carbon valencies. Do not put a hydrogen on the carboxyl carbon as well as a carbon chain, a C=O bond and an OH bond: that would exceed four bond contributions. The H written at the end of COOH belongs on oxygen.

As a quick practice comparison, CH3CH2COOH is propanoic acid whereas CH3CH2CHO is propanal. Both names include the terminal carbon, but the acid has two oxygens and the aldehyde one. The endings communicate that functional-group difference; they are not interchangeable spellings for the same molecule. Topic 4.1 introduces shared parent stems, and Topic 4.5 explains how a changed skeleton or functional group can create a structural-isomer relationship when total composition is held constant.

### Counting the acid atoms

Start with the carbon skeleton, including the carboxyl carbon and any branches. Count the two oxygens of COOH separately. Then count carbon-bound hydrogens and add the H bonded to oxygen. The carboxyl carbon of RCOOH has no H of its own when its remaining bond goes to R. In HCOOH, the simplest acid, its remaining bond goes to H instead.

For CH3CH2COOH, the methyl group supplies three hydrogens, the CH2 supplies two and OH supplies one. There are three carbons, six hydrogens and two oxygens, giving C3H6O2. For (CH3)2CHCOOH, the two methyl groups supply six hydrogens, CH supplies one and OH one, giving C4H8O2. The open-chain saturated monocarboxylic-acid relationship gives the same check for n=4.

In skeletal notation, double lines joining carbon and O represent one C=O bond to one oxygen atom, while the separate OH label identifies the second oxygen and its hydrogen. Do not count each line stroke as an atom or mistake a labelled O endpoint for an omitted carbon. A drawing's visual length does not determine its molecular size; vertices, unlabelled ends and printed atom labels do.

If requested to give a molecular formula, use actual counts. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations answer different requests: empirical C2H4O describes the simplest ratio for C4H8O2, while the structural forms can distinguish butanoic acid from 2-methylpropanoic acid. Neither molecular composition nor Mr can distinguish that pair by itself. Topic 1.1 provides the arithmetic for Mr once the correct atom count is known; connectivity remains necessary to assign the acid's name.

### Oxidation routes to acids

A primary alcohol can be oxidised through an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. For ethanol the sequence is CH3CH2OH → CH3CHO → CH3COOH. The carbon skeleton retains two carbons throughout. The first stage removes hydrogen to make C=O, while the further stage converts the aldehyde group to COOH. An extra oxygen does not imply an extra carbon.

Organic equations can represent the oxidation with [O]. Ethanol to ethanoic acid is CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O. Ethanal to the same acid is CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH. Distinguish the number of oxidation equivalents needed from the two starting materials; an aldehyde has already undergone the first oxidation stage.

Heat a primary alcohol with excess acidified dichromate(VI) under reflux when the intended endpoint is the acid. The condenser returns volatile material, allowing continued contact with oxidant. In contrast, removing the aldehyde as it forms is used to limit further oxidation when that intermediate is wanted. The oxidant changes from orange towards green as it is reduced, but the colour change alone does not establish a particular isolated organic product.

For example, complete oxidation of 0.0500 mol ethanol can give at most 0.0500 mol ethanoic acid. With Mr(acid)=60.0 the theoretical mass is 3.00 g. Actual recovery can be lower because of incomplete conversion or separation losses. A secondary alcohol normally gives a ketone under the corresponding mild oxidation route, so do not predict a same-skeleton acid from any alcohol merely because it contains OH. Topic 4.4 explains alcohol classification; Topic 4.6 explains the aldehyde intermediate and why its carbonyl attachments matter.

### Salt formation and ester formation

A carboxylic acid forms a carboxylate salt by losing its acidic hydrogen. With magnesium, 2CH3COOH + Mg → (CH3COO)2Mg + H2. The ethanoate ion has charge −1, so two are needed for Mg2+. The hydrogen gas arises from the acid's hydrogen, not from conversion of carbon into gas. Suitable reactive metals are needed; do not infer identical behaviour for any metal.

With sodium hydroxide, CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COONa + H2O. This neutralisation retains the acid's carbon skeleton. With sodium carbonate, 2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 → 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2. A carbonate therefore gives carbon dioxide effervescence, whereas the hydroxide equation does not. Balance the two acid hydrogens against the carbonate group's conversion to water and carbon dioxide.

Heating a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and an acid catalyst can form an ester. CH3COOH + CH3OH ⇌ CH3COOCH3 + H2O gives methyl ethanoate. At fixed temperature this esterification is reversible, so mixing equal amounts does not guarantee complete conversion. The catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium without determining its position at that temperature. Product amounts also depend on the starting proportions and whether a product is removed.

For an unfamiliar acid, keep RCOO together in its salt and check the metal charge. For an unfamiliar ester, identify the acid-derived carbonyl part and the alcohol-derived group attached through oxygen. These two bookkeeping methods preserve the connections rather than treating the overall composition as a list of freely rearrangeable atoms. Topic 2.3 provides equilibrium reasoning, while the next unit explains how ester names and hydrolysis reverse the connection between acid and alcohol components.

---

## Carboxylic acids and derivatives — 4.7.2

### Ester and primary-amine structures

An ester contains the connection R–C(=O)–O–R′, with a carbon group attached through the single-bonded oxygen. It differs from a carboxylic acid because that oxygen bears a carbon group instead of H. For methyl ethanoate, CH3C(=O)OCH3, the carbonyl carbon and its methyl group form the acid-derived part; the methyl group after oxygen is the alcohol-derived part.

A primary amine has one carbon-containing group attached to nitrogen and two N–H bonds: RNH2. In ethanamine, CH3CH2NH2, nitrogen makes three single bonds and has a lone pair. A molecule such as CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3 is still a primary amine because nitrogen has one carbon-group attachment, even though the carbon bearing NH2 is attached to two other carbons. Alcohol and amine classification count different centres.

Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms must preserve the requested information. Molecular and empirical formulae give actual counts and simplest ratios respectively. Structural condensed, displayed and skeletal representations retain connections. In skeletal notation write O, N and their attached H atoms explicitly. A printed NH2 endpoint is nitrogen, not an extra carbon with an omitted label.

For saturated open-chain primary monoamines without other functional groups, composition is CnH2n+3N. Saturated open-chain monoesters without other functional groups follow CnH2nO2, with n counting both sides and the carbonyl carbon. These relationships require the stated class restrictions. Equal acid and ester atom counts do not mean equal functional groups: inspect whether the single-bonded oxygen has H or carbon attached. Topic 4.3 shows primary-amine formation from a halogenoalkane; detailed additional amine reaction schemes are outside this unit's task.

### Naming the two parts correctly

Name an ester by identifying the group attached through the single-bonded oxygen first. That alcohol-derived group supplies an alkyl name, such as methyl or ethyl. The carbonyl-containing part supplies the alkanoate name from its parent acid. CH3COOCH3 is methyl ethanoate; CH3COOCH2CH3 is ethyl ethanoate. Count the acid's carbonyl carbon when choosing ethanoate, propanoate and related names.

CH3CH2COOCH3 is methyl propanoate, not propyl ethanoate. The three carbons on the acid side include C=O, while the one after oxygen gives methyl. Swapping the words without checking the connections can produce a different molecule even when the total number of carbons happens to match. To draw from a name, construct the named acid-derived C(=O)O part and then attach the specified alkyl group to its single-bonded oxygen.

The syllabus uses names such as 2-aminobutane for CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3: choose the carbon parent and number the amino attachment. The equivalent suffix style butan-2-amine identifies the same connectivity. For CH3CH2NH2 the simple name ethanamine is also used. Retain the primary NH2 arrangement regardless of naming style.

Check an amine drawing by giving nitrogen one carbon bond and two H bonds, rather than adding an extra carbon group because the carbon parent is branched. For an ester, check both the acid-derived and alcohol-derived carbon counts separately before adding them. These two habits distinguish a correct systematic name from a plausible-looking string of stems. Topic 4.1 introduces family naming, and the hydrolysis section below uses the same two ester parts to identify the products.

### Counting across oxygen or nitrogen

For an ester, count the carbonyl carbon, its attached carbon group and the group attached through oxygen. Do not stop counting when the chain reaches O. In CH3COOCH2CH3 there are four carbons: one methyl before C=O, the carbonyl carbon, then CH2 and CH3 after oxygen. Hydrogens total 3 + 0 + 2 + 3 = 8, and two oxygen atoms give C4H8O2.

For CH3CH2NH2, the carbon groups supply five hydrogens and nitrogen supplies two more, giving C2H7N. For CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3, the carbon-bound hydrogen total is 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 9; add the two N–H hydrogens to obtain C4H11N. Omitting NH2 hydrogens would incorrectly describe the composition of the stated neutral amine.

At nitrogen, draw three single bonds and a lone pair for the neutral primary examples. At an ester carbonyl carbon, C=O uses two bond contributions and the two remaining connections use one each. The single-bonded ester oxygen has two bonds and no OH hydrogen. These local checks are more reliable than guessing counts from the name's longest stem alone.

If requested for a molecular formula, give actual totals. Molecular, empirical, structural condensed, displayed and skeletal forms remain different choices: empirical C2H4O is the simplest ratio for C4H8O2, while structural representations locate the atoms. To demonstrate the count, expand a supplied skeletal ester or amine into a labelled connectivity drawing, then tally atoms once each. Topic 1.1 covers relative mass calculations; the structural count must be correct before that arithmetic can give a meaningful result.

### Hydrolysis gives different acid and base products

Hydrolysis breaks an ester connection through reaction with water. Heating with dilute aqueous acid gives the parent carboxylic acid and alcohol. For methyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH3 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + CH3OH. At fixed temperature this acid-catalysed process is reversible, corresponding to the reverse of esterification. Excess water can favour hydrolysis, but an acid catalyst alone does not guarantee total conversion.

Heating the ester with aqueous sodium hydroxide gives sodium ethanoate and methanol: CH3COOCH3 + NaOH → CH3COONa + CH3OH. The immediate acid-derived product is the carboxylate salt, not free ethanoic acid. If acid is added after hydrolysis, the carboxylate can be protonated to recover the acid. That separate step must be stated when free acid is requested from a base-hydrolysis route.

For an unfamiliar ester, draw a division between the carbonyl carbon and the single-bonded oxygen. The portion R–C(=O) becomes RCOOH in the acidic route or RCOO− in the basic route. The portion O–R′ becomes HO–R′, the alcohol. Retain the oxygen-to-alkyl connection instead of separating the ester into arbitrary equal-carbon fragments.

For CH3CH2COOCH2CH3, acid hydrolysis gives propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, and ethanol, CH3CH2OH. Base hydrolysis with NaOH gives CH3CH2COONa and the same ethanol. Both routes conserve the five original carbons across their organic products. Check water or hydroxide in the balance, product charges and any separately added acid. Topic 2.3 supplies equilibrium language for the reversible acidic route; Topic 4.4 identifies the alcohol product.

### Linking ester properties to uses

Suitable esters are used as solvents because their polar ester group and carbon-containing portions can interact favourably with a range of organic solutes. Some also evaporate readily, allowing a dissolved coating or ingredient to remain after the solvent leaves. Ethyl ethanoate is an example of an ester solvent. Solubility depends on both the particular ester and solute; the presence of an ester linkage does not make a substance dissolve every material.

Many simple low-molecular-mass esters have characteristic pleasant or fruity odours. Enough molecules enter the vapour to reach the nose, making suitable compounds useful in perfume formulations and flavouring mixtures. The property belongs to particular structures and concentrations rather than to the mere word ester. Larger or differently substituted esters can have very different volatility and odour.

An original formulation comparison might specify that solvent A dissolves a resin and evaporates at a useful rate, while solvent B leaves the resin undissolved. Those observations support A for that stated task; they do not demonstrate that A is suitable for every formulation or direct consumption. Similarly, a pleasant smell alone does not establish that an unknown liquid is an ester or that it is appropriate as a food ingredient. Chemical identity and suitability require evidence beyond odour.

Distinguish a physical use from a reaction. Dissolving resin involves solute–solvent interactions; it does not imply ester hydrolysis. A perfume's scent likewise does not require breaking its ester bond during application. Topic 1.3 provides intermolecular-interaction reasoning, Topic 4.4 describes related solvent behaviour in alcohols, and the preceding section explains the deliberate aqueous acid or base settings that actually produce hydrolysis. Keep the useful property, application and relevant limitation linked in an explanation.

# 4.7 Carboxylic acids and derivatives — practice tasks and worked answers



## ITEM-8224-4.7-P01

7 marks · Bloom: Apply

Identify the correct option in each question (1 mark each).
1. Name HCOOH. A methanoic acid; B ethanoic acid; C methanol; D methanal
2. Name CH3CH2COOH. A ethanoic acid; B propanoic acid; C butanoic acid; D propanal
3. Name CH3COOCH3. A ethyl methanoate; B methyl propanoate; C methyl ethanoate; D ethanoic acid
4. Identify the syllabus name of CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3. A 1-aminobutane; B 2-aminopropane; C butan-2-ol; D 2-aminobutane
5. Name CH3CH2COOCH2CH3. A ethyl propanoate; B propyl ethanoate; C methyl butanoate; D ethyl ethanoate
6. Name CH3(CH2)4COOH. A pentanoic acid; B hexanoic acid; C butanoic acid; D hexanol
7. Identify the name of CH3CH2NH2. A ethanol; B ethanamide; C ethanamine; D propanamine



### Worked answer

1. Key/correct option A. A has one acid carbon; B adds carbon, C loses carbonyl and D loses acid OH. Each distractor represents the specified error.
2. Key/correct option B. B includes the acid carbon; A omits it, C adds one and D changes functional group. Each distractor represents the specified error.
3. Key/correct option C. C correctly names both sides; A swaps their counts, B adds acid carbon and D loses the ester alkyl group. Each distractor represents the specified error.
4. Key/correct option D. D preserves four carbons and NH2 position; A moves it, B loses carbon and C changes the group. Each distractor represents the specified error.
5. Key/correct option A. A identifies ethyl on O and propanoate on the carbonyl side; B/C change connectivity and D misses a carbon. Each distractor represents the specified error.
6. Key/correct option B. B counts methyl plus four CH2 plus carboxyl carbon; A/C undercount and D changes family. Each distractor represents the specified error.
7. Key/correct option C. C describes two carbons and NH2; A changes heteroatom, B adds a carbonyl group and D adds carbon. Each distractor represents the specified error.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: key, correct option, distractor, error. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-4.7-P02

8 marks · Bloom: Apply

Explain structural naming in CH3CH2COOH and CH3CH2COOCH3.
(a) Name the acid and draw its functional-group bonds. [3]
(b) Give the acid molecular composition. [1]
(c) Name the ester and identify the parent acid and alcohol from its two portions. [3]
(d) Name CH3CH(NH2)CH2CH3 using the amino-prefix style. [1]



### Worked answer

(a) Propanoic acid [1]; carbonyl C=O [1] and C–O–H on the same carbon [1]. (b) C3H6O2 [1]. (c) Methyl propanoate [1]; propanoic acid supplies carbonyl portion [1], methanol supplies O–CH3 portion [1]. (d) 2-aminobutane [1]. Creditworthy points per part, total8 marks.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: part, mark, creditworthy point. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.



## ITEM-8224-4.7-P03

5 marks · Bloom: Apply

Calculate the maximum acid mass from complete oxidation of 2.30 g ethanol with excess acidified dichromate(VI) under reflux. Name the product, draw its carboxyl connection and give molecular composition. Mr(ethanol)=46.0; Ar(C)=12.0, Ar(H)=1.0, Ar(O)=16.0. [5]



### Worked answer

Ethanoic acid, CH3C(=O)OH, C2H4O2 [1]. Equation: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O [1]. Working: n(ethanol)=2.30/46.0=0.0500 mol [1]; ratio1:1 gives0.0500 mol acid, Mr=2(12.0)+4(1.0)+2(16.0)=60.0 [1]; m=0.0500×60.0=3.00 g [1]. Answer to three significant figures; masses already in g so no prefix conversion is needed.



### Marking guidance

Required answer parts: equation, working, answer, unit, significant figures. Use the specific chemically correct points in the canonical answer; award no additional credit for repetition.
